doc_description: PepsiCo, Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10‑K for the fiscal year ended December 25, 2021—covering its seven global food and beverage segments and pep+ sustainability strategy, KPMG‑audited financials and MD&A, extensive risk factors (e.g., COVID‑19, supply chain, packaging and taxes), and key portfolio moves including the Q1 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to a PAI Partners JV (with a retained 39% stake), along with detailed pension equalization and international retirement plan appendices.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:

- Lists securities registered under Section 12(b) (common stock and multiple senior notes with trading symbols and maturities) and notes no Section 12(g) securities.
- Includes required Exchange Act checkboxes: well-known seasoned issuer; filing compliance; electronic data submission; large accelerated filer status; Section 404(b) auditor attestation of internal control; not a shell company.
- Provides market value of non-affiliate common stock as of the second fiscal quarter and shares outstanding as of a recent date.
- Notes incorporation by reference of the 2022 Proxy Statement into Part III.
- Presents the Table of Contents for Parts I–IV, covering Business, Risk Factors, Properties, Legal Proceedings, Mine Safety, Market for Equity and Issuer Purchases, MD&A, Market Risk, Financial Statements, Controls and Procedures, Other Information (including foreign jurisdictions that prevent inspections), and governance, compensation, ownership, related-party matters, auditor fees, exhibits, and a Form 10-K summary.

- Begins Item 1. Business: defines terminology, references a glossary, and provides a company overview—PepsiCo as a leading global beverage and convenient foods company (Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Quaker, SodaStream), operating via company operations, authorized bottlers, contract manufacturers, and third parties in 200+ countries and territories.
- Describes organizational structure into seven reportable segments and lists those shown: Frito-Lay North America (U.S./Canada convenient foods), Quaker Foods North America (U.S./Canada cereals and other foods), PepsiCo Beverages North America (U.S./Canada beverages), Latin America (beverages and convenient foods), and Europe (beverages and convenient foods).

nodes.title: Company Overview
nodes.heading: Company Overview
nodes.start_phrase: We were incorporated in Delaware in 1919 and reincorporated in North Carolina in 1986.
nodes.summary:
- Standard forward-looking statements disclaimer for a Form 10-K, noting use of predictive terms, inherent risks and uncertainties, references to Item 1A Risk Factors and Item 7 MD&A for details, caution against undue reliance, and no obligation to update.
- Introduction to Part I, Item 1 (Business), clarifying that “we,” “us,” “our,” “PepsiCo,” and the “Company” refer to PepsiCo, Inc. and its consolidated subsidiaries, with certain terms defined in a Glossary in Item 7.
- Company overview: incorporated in Delaware (1919), reincorporated in North Carolina (1986); positioned as a leading global beverage and convenient foods company with key brands including Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Quaker, and SodaStream; products made, marketed, distributed, and sold through company operations, authorized bottlers, contract manufacturers, and other third parties in over 200 countries and territories.
- Operations structured into seven reportable segments, with five listed and described:
  1) Frito-Lay North America (FLNA) – branded convenient foods in the U.S. and Canada.
  2) Quaker Foods North America (QFNA) – branded convenient foods (e.g., cereal, rice, pasta) in the U.S. and Canada.
  3) PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA) – beverage businesses in the U.S. and Canada.
  4) Latin America (LatAm) – beverage and convenient foods across Latin America.
  5) Europe – beverage and convenient foods across Europe.

nodes.title: Our Operations
nodes.heading: Our Operations
nodes.start_phrase: We are or ganized into seven reportable segments (also referred to as divisions), as follows:
nodes.summary:
- Forward-looking statements disclaimer under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, including identifying language, risk awareness, references to Item 1A Risk Factors and MD&A, and a note that the company undertakes no obligation to update such statements.
- Introduction to Part I, Item 1. Business, and definition of terms used (e.g., “we,” “PepsiCo”) with a reference to a glossary in Item 7.
- Company overview: PepsiCo’s incorporation history (1919 Delaware; 1986 North Carolina), positioning as a leading global beverage and convenient foods company, major brands (Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Gatorade, Pepsi-Cola, Mountain Dew, Quaker, SodaStream), and worldwide operations across 200+ countries via company operations, authorized bottlers, contract manufacturers, and other partners.
- Organizational structure: seven reportable segments—Frito-Lay North America (FLNA), Quaker Foods North America (QFNA), PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA), Latin America (LatAm), Europe, Africa/Middle East/South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific/Australia/New Zealand/China Region (APAC).
- FLNA: production, marketing, distribution, and sales of branded snack foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos) and dips; sales to independent distributors and retailers; Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads via joint venture with Strauss Group.
- QFNA: branded convenient foods including cereals, rice, pasta, granola bars, oatmeal, grits, rice cakes, syrups/mixes, and side dishes (e.g., Quaker, Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Rice-A-Roni); sales to independent distributors and retailers.
- PBNA: beverages in the U.S. and Canada, including concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods (Aquafina, Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Propel); own bottling and distribution plus sales to and through authorized/independent bottlers; RTD tea and coffee via JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; manufacturing/distribution under licenses from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray.
- PBNA portfolio change: 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and other select juice brands to PAI Partners; PepsiCo retains a 39% noncontrolling interest in a North America/Europe joint venture and acts as exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice for chilled DSD.
- Latin America segment: production, marketing, distribution, and sales of convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Mabel, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker-branded foods) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy); routes to market via authorized/independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers; RTD tea JV with Unilever (Lipton).
- Brief mention of remaining segments (Europe, AMESA, APAC) as comprehensive beverage and convenient food businesses in their respective geographies, with detailed descriptions not included in the provided excerpt.

nodes.title: Frito-Lay North America
nodes.heading: Frito-Lay North America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independentl y or in conjunction with third parties, FLNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods.
nodes.summary:
- Defines two international segments: AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China), each encompassing both beverage and convenient food businesses.
- Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): Produces and sells leading snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos, branded dips) primarily through independent distributors and retailers; includes the Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads joint venture with Strauss Group.
- Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): Produces and sells cereals, oatmeal, grits, granola bars, rice cakes, syrups/mixes and side dishes under brands such as Quaker, Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company and Rice-A-Roni, through independent distributors and retailers.
- PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): Produces and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups and finished goods for brands including Pepsi, Diet Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Diet Mountain Dew, Aquafina, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero and Propel; operates bottling plants and distribution facilities; sells directly and via authorized/independent bottlers. Engages in ready-to-drink tea and coffee joint ventures with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses certain brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray. Notes the 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest and serving as exclusive U.S. distributor for small-format and foodservice chilled DSD.
- Latin America (LatAm): Produces and sells snack brands (Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Mabel, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos) and Quaker-branded convenient foods; beverages include 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos and Toddy; routes to market include authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors and retailers; participates in an international Lipton RTD tea joint venture with Unilever.

nodes.title: Quaker Foods North America
nodes.heading: Quaker Foods North America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, QFNA makes, markets, distributes and sells branded convenient foods, which include cereals, rice, pasta and other branded products.
nodes.summary:
- Defines two international reporting segments: AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia) and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China).
- Outlines Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): manufactures and sells major snack brands (Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles, Tostitos, Fritos) and dips; products sold to independent distributors and retailers; Sabra refrigerated dips via joint venture with Strauss Group.
- Details Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): produces cereals, oatmeal, granola bars, rice/pasta sides and syrups/mixes under brands such as Quaker, Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company; sold to independent distributors and retailers.
- Describes PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): makes and sells concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished beverages (Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Diet variants, Aquafina, Gatorade, Propel); operates own bottling and distribution; also supplies authorized/independent bottlers; RTD tea/coffee via JVs with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; licenses brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray.
- Notes 2022 juice transaction: sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners; PepsiCo retains 39% noncontrolling interest in a new JV operating in North America and Europe; PepsiCo is exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice for the JV’s chilled DSD portfolio.
- Summarizes Latin America (LatAm): manufactures and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Sabritas, Gamesa/Mabel/Emperador cookies, Quaker foods) and beverages (e.g., Pepsi, Pepsi Black, 7UP, Mirinda, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, San Carlos, Toddy); routes to market include authorized/independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers; RTD tea via Unilever Lipton JV.
- Emphasizes go-to-market models across segments: company-operated bottling and distribution in PBNA, plus extensive use of independent distributors, retailers, and authorized/independent bottlers.

nodes.title: PepsiCo Beverages North America
nodes.heading: PepsiCo Beverages North America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, PBNA makes, markets and sells beverage concentrates, fountain syrups and finished goods under various beverage brands including Aquafina, Diet Mountain Dew, Diet Pepsi, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Mountain Dew, Pepsi and Propel.
nodes.summary:
- Defines global operating segments, including:
  - AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia): beverage and convenient food businesses.
  - APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand, and China Region): beverage and convenient food businesses.
- Frito-Lay North America (FLNA): manufactures, markets, distributes and sells branded snacks (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Fritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Tostitos, branded dips); products sold to independent distributors and retailers; JV with Strauss Group for Sabra refrigerated dips and spreads.
- Quaker Foods North America (QFNA): manufactures, markets, distributes and sells cereals, grains and convenient foods (e.g., Cap’n Crunch, Life, Pearl Milling Company, Quaker oatmeal, Chewy bars, grits, rice cakes, Simply Granola, Rice-A-Roni); sold to independent distributors and retailers.
- PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA): produces beverage concentrates, fountain syrups and finished goods (e.g., Aquafina, Mountain Dew, Diet Pepsi, Gatorade, Gatorade Zero, Pepsi, Propel); operates bottling plants and distribution; sells directly and via authorized/independent bottlers; JVs for RTD tea and coffee with Unilever (Lipton) and Starbucks; manufactures/distributes licensed brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and licensed juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray.
- Juice portfolio transaction: in 2022, sold Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners; retained 39% noncontrolling interest in a joint venture operating in North America and Europe; PepsiCo is exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice customers for chilled DSD.
- Latin America (LatAm): makes, markets, distributes and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador, Lay’s, Mabel, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas, Tostitos, Quaker-branded) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Gatorade, H2oh!, Manzanita Sol, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Black, San Carlos, Toddy); products sold via authorized and independent bottlers, independent distributors and retailers; RTD tea through Unilever (Lipton) JV.
- Overall themes: product portfolios by segment, manufacturing and distribution models (including bottling operations and independent distributors/retailers), and key joint ventures and licensing arrangements.

nodes.title: Latin America
nodes.heading: Latin America
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, LatAm makes, markets, distributes and sells a number of convenient food brand s including Cheetos, Doritos, Emperador , Lay’s, Mabel, Marias Gamesa, Ruffles, Sabritas, Saladitas and Tostitos, as well as many Quaker -branded convenient foods.
nodes.summary:
- The document outlines PepsiCo’s global operating structure and brand portfolio across six reportable segments: Frito-Lay North America (FLNA), Quaker Foods North America (QFNA), PepsiCo Beverages North America (PBNA), Latin America (LatAm), Europe, Africa/Middle East/South Asia (AMESA), and Asia Pacific/Australia/New Zealand/China (APAC).
- For each segment, it details core product categories (convenient foods and beverages), key brands (e.g., Lay’s, Doritos, Cheetos, Ruffles, Tostitos, Quaker, Pepsi, Mountain Dew, Gatorade, 7UP, Aquafina), and primary sales channels (independent distributors and retailers).
- PBNA-specific activities include operating bottling plants and distribution facilities; selling concentrates, fountain syrups, and finished goods; joint ventures for ready-to-drink tea (Unilever/Lipton) and coffee (Starbucks); and licensing/manufacturing certain brands from Keurig Dr Pepper (Crush, Dr Pepper, Schweppes) and juice brands from Dole and Ocean Spray.
- A major strategic transaction is highlighted: in Q1 2022, PepsiCo sold Tropicana, Naked, and select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a new joint venture operating in North America and Europe; PepsiCo remains the exclusive U.S. distributor to small-format and foodservice customers for chilled DSD.
- Regional specifics:
  - LatAm: snacks (e.g., Sabritas, Emperador, Marias Gamesa) and beverages (Pepsi, Pepsi Black, Mirinda, Manzanita Sol, Gatorade), plus Lipton RTD tea JV.
  - Europe: snacks (Walkers, Chipita), beverages (Pepsi, Pepsi Max, 7UP), SodaStream sparkling water makers, dairy brands (Agusha, Chudo, Domik v Derevne), select owned bottling, and Lipton RTD tea JV.
  - AMESA: snacks (Chipsy, Kurkure, Lay’s; grains brands like Sasko, Spekko, White Star), beverages (Pepsi, 7UP, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Aquafina), select owned bottling, and Lipton RTD tea JV.
  - APAC: snacks (Lay’s, Cheetos, Doritos, Smith’s, BaiCaoWei), beverages (Pepsi, 7UP, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Sting), Lipton RTD tea JV, and licensing of Tropicana for co-branded juices in China via alliance with Tingyi.
- Joint ventures and partnerships also include Sabra refrigerated dips (with Strauss Group) under FLNA.
- The distribution network overview explains use of direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse, distributor networks, and e-commerce, chosen based on customer needs, product characteristics, and local trade practices.

nodes.title: Europe
nodes.heading: Europe
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, Europe makes, markets, distributes and sells a number of convenient food brands including Cheetos, Chipita, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles and Walkers, as well as many Quaker -branded convenient foods, through consolidated businesses, as well as through noncontrolled affiliates.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines the company’s regional operations and distribution model. It details how Europe, AMESA (Africa, Middle East and South Asia), and APAC (Asia Pacific, Australia/New Zealand and China) produce, market, distribute and sell convenient foods (e.g., Lay’s, Doritos, Quaker, regional brands) and beverages (e.g., Pepsi, 7UP, Mirinda, Mountain Dew), often via both consolidated businesses and noncontrolled affiliates, and sometimes through company-operated bottling plants. It highlights partnerships and portfolio moves, including the Lipton ready-to-drink tea joint venture with Unilever across regions, Europe’s SodaStream and dairy businesses, the 2022 sale of Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners with a retained 39% noncontrolling interest in a new JV for North America and Europe, and APAC’s licensing of the Tropicana brand in China via a strategic alliance with Tingyi. The distribution network section explains multi-channel go-to-market approaches—direct-store-delivery, customer warehouse, distributor networks, and e-commerce—selected based on customer needs, product characteristics and local trade practices.

nodes.title: Africa, Middle East and South Asia
nodes.heading: Africa, Middle East and South Asia
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, AMESA makes, mark ets, distributes and sells a number of convenient food brands including Chipsy , Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko and White Star, as well as many Quaker -branded convenient foods, through consolidated businesses, as well as through noncontrolled affiliates.
nodes.summary:
- Regional operations overview: The excerpt outlines PepsiCo’s activities across three regions—Europe; Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA); and Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China (APAC)—highlighting that, either independently or with partners/noncontrolled affiliates, the company manufactures, markets, distributes and sells snack foods and beverages, and in some cases operates its own bottling and distribution facilities.

- Europe: Sells convenient foods (Cheetos, Chipita, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Walkers, Quaker) and beverages (7UP, Diet Pepsi, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Max) via authorized/independent bottlers, distributors and retailers; operates bottling/distribution in select markets. Also manufactures and distributes SodaStream products, sells dairy brands (Agusha, Chudo, Domik v Derevne), and offers ready-to-drink tea via a Lipton joint venture with Unilever. In 2022, sold Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a new JV operating in North America and Europe.

- AMESA: Offers snacks (Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, White Star, Quaker) and beverages (7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi), distributed through bottlers, distributors and retailers, with some company-operated bottling. Also sells ready-to-drink tea via the Lipton JV with Unilever.

- APAC: Provides snacks (BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Smith’s, Quaker) and beverages (7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, Sting) through bottlers, distributors and retailers; participates in the Lipton ready-to-drink tea JV. Licenses the Tropicana brand for co-branded juices in China via a strategic alliance with Tingyi.

- Distribution network: Products reach market through direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse and distributor networks, and are also sold directly to consumers via e-commerce and retailers. Channel choice depends on customer needs, product characteristics and local trade practices.

nodes.title: Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region
nodes.heading: Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China Region
nodes.start_phrase: Either independently or in conjunction with third parties, APAC makes, markets, distributes and sells a number of convenient food brands includi ng BaiCaoW ei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s and Smith’ s, as well as many Quaker -branded convenient foods, through consolidated businesses, as well as through noncontrolled affiliates.
nodes.summary:
- Regional operations overview:
  - Europe: Produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Walkers, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Diet Pepsi, Mirinda, Pepsi, Pepsi Max); operates both through consolidated businesses and noncontrolled affiliates. Also manufactures SodaStream products and sells dairy brands (Agusha, Chudo, Domik v Derevne). Participates in a Lipton RTD tea joint venture with Unilever. Sold Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands in Q1 2022 to PAI Partners, retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a JV for North America and Europe.
  - Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA): Produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, White Star, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi), via consolidated businesses and affiliates; in some markets operates own bottling and distribution. Participates in Lipton RTD tea JV with Unilever.
  - Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China (APAC): Produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Smith’s, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, Sting) via consolidated businesses and affiliates; participates in Lipton RTD tea JV with Unilever. Licenses the Tropicana brand in China for co-branded juices through a strategic alliance with Tingyi.

- Go-to-market and bottling model:
  - Beverages include concentrates, fountain syrups and finished goods sold to authorized/independent bottlers, distributors and retailers; in certain markets the company operates its own bottling plants and distribution facilities.

- Distribution network:
  - Products reach market via direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse, distributor networks, and e-commerce; channel choice depends on customer needs, product characteristics and local trade practices.

nodes.title: Our Distribution Network
nodes.heading: Our Distribution Network
nodes.start_phrase: Our products are primarily brought to market through direct-store-delivery (DSD), customer warehouse and distributor networks and are also sold directly to consumers through e-commerce platforms and retailers.
nodes.summary:
- Regional operations and product portfolio:
  - Europe: Produces and sells convenient foods (e.g., Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Ruffles, Walkers, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Pepsi, Pepsi Max), via consolidated businesses and noncontrolled affiliates; sells to authorized/independent bottlers, distributors, and retailers; operates some own bottling; manufactures and distributes SodaStream; offers dairy brands (Agusha, Chudo, Domik v Derevne); markets RTD tea via Lipton JV with Unilever; sold Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners in Q1 2022, retaining a 39% stake in a new JV operating in North America and Europe.
  - Africa, Middle East and South Asia (AMESA): Produces convenient foods (e.g., Chipsy, Doritos, Kurkure, Lay’s, Sasko, Spekko, White Star, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi); sells through bottlers, distributors, and retailers; operates some own bottling; markets RTD tea via Lipton JV.
  - Asia Pacific, Australia and New Zealand and China (APAC): Produces convenient foods (e.g., BaiCaoWei, Cheetos, Doritos, Lay’s, Smith’s, Quaker) and beverages (e.g., 7UP, Aquafina, Mirinda, Mountain Dew, Pepsi, Sting); sells via bottlers, distributors, and retailers; markets RTD tea via Lipton JV; licenses Tropicana for co-branded juice in China via alliance with Tingyi.

- Distribution network:
  - Direct-store-delivery (DSD) for high-visibility, frequently restocked products.
  - Customer warehouse deliveries from company/third-party plants and distribution centers for less fragile, lower-turnover items.
  - Third-party distributor networks, including foodservice and vending channels to restaurants, businesses, schools, and stadiums.
  - E-commerce sales through company-owned and third-party platforms/apps.

- Ingredients, packaging, and supplies:
  - Key inputs: various fruit juices/concentrates, sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, corn sweeteners, sugar), grains (corn, oats, rice, wheat, flour), potatoes, raw milk, seasonings, oils, water.
  - Packaging: PET and polypropylene resins, film, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, paperboard; emphasis on recyclability and increased recycled content (including recycled PET).
  - Energy needs: fuel, electricity, natural gas for operations and logistics.

- Supply chain and risk management:
  - Use of specialists, multiple geographies/suppliers, and open-market purchasing.
  - Price risk managed via fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements, and derivatives (swaps, futures).
  - Selective pass-through of cost increases to customers.
  - Ongoing investments in sustainable agricultural practices and global expansion of supplier sustainability initiatives.

- Recent operating environment:
  - In 2021 and into fiscal 2022, higher than anticipated costs for commodities, packaging, and other inputs, and some limited shortages due to inflation, supply chain disruptions, labor shortages, increased demand, and COVID-19 impacts.

nodes.title: Direct-Store-Delivery
nodes.heading: Direct-Store-Delivery
nodes.start_phrase: We, our independen t bottlers and our distributors operate DSD systems that deliver beverages and convenient foods directly to retail stores where the products are merchandised by our employees or our independent bottlers.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines the company’s go-to-market and supply strategies. It details four distribution channels: Direct-Store-Delivery (for high-visibility, frequently restocked items merchandised in-store), Customer Warehouse (cost-efficient delivery for less fragile, lower-turnover products), third-party Distributor Networks (to extend reach, notably in foodservice and vending for restaurants, businesses, schools, and stadiums), and growing E-commerce (company-owned and third-party platforms). It lists primary ingredients (various fruit juices and concentrates, grains, sweeteners like aspartame and sucralose, oils, seasonings, dairy, and water) and key packaging materials (PET, polypropylene, films, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, paperboard), emphasizing recyclability and increased use of recycled content such as rPET. Energy inputs (fuel, electricity, natural gas) are highlighted as critical. The company manages supply and price volatility via specialists, diversified sourcing across geographies and suppliers, and financial/contractual tools (fixed-price contracts, pricing agreements, swaps, futures), with no significant continuous shortages reported. It continues investing in sustainable agriculture and supplier farming practices globally. nodes.summary:

  - Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD) for frequent-restock, promotion-responsive products with in-store merchandising.

- Ingredients, packaging, and supply chain:
  - Key inputs include various juices and concentrates, sweeteners (corn sweeteners, sugar, aspartame, sucralose), grains (oats, wheat, rice, flour), potatoes, dairy, oils, seasonings, and water.
  - Packaging materials include PET and polypropylene resins, films, aluminum, glass, closures, cardboard, and paperboard, with an emphasis on recyclability and increased recycled content (e.g., rPET).

- Brands and intellectual property:

nodes.summary:
- Supply chain finance: Voluntary programs with global financial institutions allow suppliers to sell PepsiCo receivables; arrangements had no material impact; further details referenced in MD&A liquidity section.
- Brands and intellectual property: Extensive global trademark portfolio across beverages and convenient foods; long-term trademark licenses (e.g., Ocean Spray); distribution of third-party brands (e.g., Bang Energy, select Keurig Dr Pepper brands); JV- and partner-related trademarks (Lipton, Sabra, Starbucks). Sold Tropicana, Naked and select juice brands to PAI Partners, retaining a 39% noncontrolling interest in a JV operating in North America and Europe; PepsiCo is the exclusive U.S. distributor for certain channels. Beginning 2022, distribution of Hard MTN Dew under license to Boston Beer. Active trademark governance and merchandising licensing; ownership and licensing of patents covering products, packaging, processes, and equipment.
- Seasonality: Beverage and snack sales peak in Q3 and are lowest in Q1; seasonality not material to consolidated results overall.
- Customers and routes to market: Broad customer base across wholesale, foodservice, retail, e-commerce, discounters, and independent bottlers. Exclusive bottling and distribution agreements define territories, quality standards, and allow PepsiCo to charge for concentrate, finished goods, and Aquafina royalties. Use of financial incentives (rebates, placement fees, promotions, displays); “bottler funding” supports consumer incentives, advertising, new product launches, and placement of vending/cooler equipment; programs vary annually. Market shifts (retail consolidation, e-commerce/omnichannel growth, hard discounters, COVID-19 effects) heighten reliance on major customers; Walmart accounted for ~13% of 2021 net revenue; loss would materially impact FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA.
- Competition: Highly competitive categories versus global, regional, local, private-label, and direct-to-consumer microbrands; The Coca-Cola Company is the primary beverage competitor; other major competitors include Campbell, Conagra, Hormel, Kellogg, Keurig Dr Pepper, Kraft Heinz, Jack Link’s, Mondelēz, Monster, Nestlé, Red Bull, and Utz. PepsiCo holds leading positions in many convenient food categories; in 2021, PepsiCo and Coca-Cola represented approximately 22% and 19%, respectively, of U.S. liquid refreshment beverage retail sales in measured channels (IRI).

nodes.title: Our Customers
nodes.heading: Our Customers
nodes.start_phrase: Our custom ers inclu de wholesale and other distributors, foodservice customers, grocery stores, drug stores, convenience stores, discount/dollar stores, mass merchandisers, membership stores, hard discounters, e-commerce retailers and authorized independent bottlers , among others.
nodes.summary:

- Explains bottler relationships: typically exclusive territorial contracts to manufacture and/or distribute trademarked beverages; company retains rights to charge for concentrate, finished goods, and Aquafina royalties; specifies required manufacturing processes and quality standards.
- Details customer and bottler incentives: volume rebates, placement fees, promotions, displays; “bottler funding” negotiated annually to support consumer incentives, advertising/media, new product launches, and vending/cooler equipment placement; programs vary year to year.
- Highlights retail landscape shifts: consolidation of retailers, growth of e-commerce and mobile commerce (including subscriptions and DTC), omnichannel integration, international expansion of hard discounters, and effects of the COVID‑19 environment—raising the importance of major customers.
- Notes customer concentration risk: Walmart (including Sam’s Club) accounted for ~13% of 2021 consolidated net revenue across divisions (including concentrate sold to bottlers for Walmart-bound finished goods); loss would materially affect FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA.
- Outlines competitive environment: intense competition from global, regional, local, private label, and micro-brand players selling via e-commerce and local-focused retailers; The Coca-Cola Company is the primary beverage competitor.
- Lists key competitors across beverages and convenient foods: Coca-Cola, Campbell Soup, Conagra, Hormel, Kellogg, Keurig Dr Pepper, Kraft Heinz, Link Snacks, Mondelēz, Monster, Nestlé, Red Bull, Utz, among others.

nodes.title: Our Competition
nodes.heading: Our Competition
nodes.start_phrase: Our beverage and convenient food products are in highly competitive categori es and markets and compete against products of international beverage and convenient food companies that, like us, operate in multiple geographies, as well as regional, local and private label manufacturers and economy brands and other competitors, inclu ding smaller companies developing and selling micro brands directl y to consumers through e-commerce platforms or through retailers focused on locally-sourced products.
nodes.summary:
- Customers: Broad base spanning wholesalers, distributors, foodservice, and multiple retail channels (grocery, drug, convenience, mass, club, hard discounters, e-commerce), plus authorized independent bottlers. Company grants independent bottlers exclusive geographic manufacturing and distribution rights for certain trademarked beverages, charges for concentrate/finished goods/Aquafina royalties, and sets quality processes. Provides extensive customer and bottler incentives (rebates, placement fees, promotions, advertising support, new product support, vending/cooler equipment), negotiated annually. Retail consolidation, e-commerce growth, omni-retail integration, hard discounter expansion, and COVID-19 heighten dependence on major customers; Walmart represented ~13% of 2021 consolidated net revenue, and its loss would materially affect FLNA, QFNA, and PBNA.

- Competition: Highly competitive beverage and convenient food markets against global, regional, local, private-label, and direct-to-consumer players. The Coca-Cola Company is the primary beverage competitor; other named competitors span snacks, beverages, and packaged foods. Company holds strong leadership in many convenient food categories; in 2021, it held ~22% of U.S. liquid refreshment beverage retail sales vs. Coca-Cola’s ~19%, while Coca-Cola leads in CSDs outside the U.S. Key competition factors include brand strength, taste, price/value, quality, variety, innovation, distribution, digital marketing, packaging, convenience, service, and responsiveness to health, wellness, sustainability, and e-commerce trends. Success depends on effective promotion, innovation and reformulation, production efficiency, digital/technology adoption, packaging/pricing, equipment, and brand/trademark protection.

- Research and development: Global investment to meet customer/consumer needs and drive growth. Focus areas include new technologies, ingredients, flavors, substrates; manufacturing improvements to cut cost and environmental footprint; reducing added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat; expanding functional/positive nutrition offerings; sustainable packaging (less plastic, recyclable/compostable/biodegradable); marketing/merchandising/dispensing equipment; “beyond the bottle” solutions (e.g., SodaStream); digitalization with AI and data analytics; omnichannel and e-commerce capabilities; and reducing water use and climate impact across the value chain. Research centers operate across multiple countries.

- Regulatory matters: Business activities across the product lifecycle, employment/occupational safety, and data protection are subject to extensive laws and regulations in the U.S. and in 200+ other countries and territories. Company policy is global compliance with applicable laws and regulations.

nodes.title: Research and Development
nodes.heading: Resear ch and Development
nodes.start_phrase: We engage in a variety of research and development activities and invest in innovation globally with the goal of meeting the needs of our custom ers and consumers and accelerating growth.
nodes.summary:
- Competitive landscape and positioning: The company notes a significant carbonated soft drink (CSD) share advantage in many non-U.S. markets. It competes on brand strength, taste, price/value, quality, innovation, distribution, digital and traditional marketing, packaging, convenience, and service, while rapidly responding to health/wellness, sustainability, and e-commerce trends. Success factors include strong promotion, new product launches and reformulations, production efficiency, technology integration, effective advertising, pricing, vending/dispensing advancements, and brand/trademark protection.

- Research and development strategy: Global investment to drive growth through consumer-preferred product innovation, new technologies, ingredients, flavors, and substrates; manufacturing process improvements to cut costs and environmental impact.

- Health and nutrition priorities: Reformulations to reduce added sugars, sodium, and saturated fat; expansion of products with functional ingredients and “positive nutrition” (whole grains, fruits/vegetables, dairy, protein, fiber, micronutrients, hydration).

- Packaging and sustainability: Development of packaging technologies and designs that reduce plastic and advance recyclable, compostable, biodegradable, or otherwise sustainable solutions; expansion of beyond-the-bottle offerings, including SodaStream.

- Technology and digitalization: Use of AI and data analytics to enhance consumer insights and research; strengthening omnichannel capabilities, especially e-commerce; development of marketing, merchandising, and dispensing equipment.

- Environmental stewardship: Efforts to reduce water use in operations and agriculture and to lower climate impact across the value chain.

- Global R&D footprint: Research centers in Brazil, China, India, Ireland, Mexico, Russia, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and the United States, leveraging consumer insights, food science, and engineering for beverage and convenient food innovation.

- Regulatory compliance: Operations across the product lifecycle and in employment, safety, and data protection are subject to extensive laws and regulations in the U.S. and in 200+ countries/territories; the company’s policy is to comply with applicable laws worldwide.

nodes.heading: The impact of COVID-19 continues to create considerable uncertainty for our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Our global operations continue to expo se us to risks associated with the COVID-19 pandemic.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) as a competitive advantage, with workforce representation data: 27% female globally, 43% female in management; in the U.S., 45% racially/ethnically diverse overall and 31% in managerial roles; CEO’s direct reports include seven diverse and/or female executives.

- Introduction to Item 1A. Risk Factors, noting that listed risks may materially affect the business and stock price and are not exhaustive.
- Business risks related to COVID-19: ongoing uncertainty; changes in consumer demand and channel mix (notably increased e-commerce); potential customer financial distress; operational disruptions from facility closures and workforce availability; supply chain challenges (materials, labor, transportation, port congestion, border issues); higher costs (employee support, PPE, sanitation, credit losses, inventory write-offs, and input cost inflation); heightened IT load and cyber risk from remote work; and capital/credit market volatility.
- Acknowledgment that COVID-19 amplifies other risks and that future impacts depend on virus variants, vaccine/treatment effectiveness and uptake, government actions, macroeconomic conditions, and potentially lasting consumer behavior changes.
- Risk of reduced future demand tied to the need for continuous innovation and responsiveness to evolving consumer preferences, including demographics, consumption patterns, channel shifts (e-commerce and online-to-offline), pricing and quality expectations, environmental concerns about packaging (e.g., single-use plastics), and health/nutrition or ingredient-origin perceptions influenced by third-party studies, which could lead to decreased purchases or boycotts.

nodes.title: Reduction in future demand for our products would adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Reduction in future demand for our products would adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Demand for our products depends in part on our ability to innovate and anticipate and effectively respond to shifts in consumer trends and preferenc es, including the types of products our consumers want and how they browse for, purchase and consume them.
nodes.summary:
- COVID-19 impacts on demand and channels: illness, quarantines, store closures, and consumer financial hardship; accelerated shift to e-commerce affecting sales mix and profitability; customer credit risk and potential bankruptcies.
- Operational and supply chain disruptions: facility and partner shutdowns; workforce unavailability (illness, absenteeism, vaccine mandates, travel restrictions); shortages of raw materials, packaging, labor, and transport; port congestion and border restrictions; sustained interruptions harming operations.
- Cost pressures: higher employee and operating costs (benefits, incentives, PPE, sanitation), credit loss allowances, upfront payment reserves, inventory write-offs, and inflation in commodities, packaging, and transportation, all weighing on profitability.
- Technology and financing risks: increased remote work straining IT infrastructure and elevating cyberattack exposure; volatility in capital and credit markets limiting access to financing on acceptable terms.
- Ongoing pandemic uncertainty: impact contingent on variant emergence, vaccine/treatment availability and efficacy, rollout speed, government responses, macroeconomic conditions, and potentially lasting shifts in consumer behavior.
- Future demand risk from changing consumer preferences: need to innovate and respond to shifts in demographics, channels (including e-commerce and online-to-offline), pricing sensitivity, product quality expectations, environmental and packaging concerns (e.g., single-use plastics), health/nutrition and ingredient-origin perceptions (including third-party studies), and brand/marketing effectiveness (especially digital and social media). Inadequate response or underinvestment (e.g., in data analytics) could erode demand and lead to write-offs.
- External event vulnerability: natural disasters or uncontrollable events can disrupt supply chains and product availability; ineffective crisis management could depress demand.
- Reputation and brand image risks: potential damage from lapses in ethics or ESG (human rights, child labor, DEI, workplace health and safety), failure to meet ESG goals (nutrition profile, packaging, water use, environmental impact), health concerns about products (e.g., obesity), product quality/safety issues, regulatory noncompliance, and negative reactions to advertising, sponsorships, social media, or responses to political/social events; poor management of negative commentary can further harm demand.
- Product quality and safety/recalls: risks from mislabeling, misbranding, spoilage, undeclared allergens, adulteration, and contamination leading to recalls, costs, inventory destruction, lost sales, delivery disruptions, fines/judgments, and reputational harm; heightened exposure as the company expands into nuts, meat convenient foods, and U.S. alcoholic beverage distribution. Insufficient oversight can trigger litigation, investigations, and potential civil/criminal liability; broad consumer loss of confidence in product integrity can adversely affect the business.

nodes.title: Damage to our reputation or brand image can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Damage to our reputation or brand image can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Maintaining a positive reputation globally is critical to selling our products.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on risk factors affecting a consumer products company’s performance and demand.
- Shifting consumer preferences and trends driven by brand perception, effectiveness of advertising/marketing, and engagement via digital and social media; failure to anticipate or respond (including via data analytics) can erode demand, lead to inventory write-offs, and weaken competitive and financial position.
- Operational vulnerability to natural disasters and other uncontrollable events that can disrupt the supply chain; reliance on effective crisis management to maintain product availability and demand.
- Reputation and brand image risks tied to ethical, business, and ESG practices (human rights, child labor, DEI, workplace conditions, health and safety); achievement of ESG goals (nutrition profile, packaging, water use, environmental impact).
- Health-related concerns about products or ingredients (e.g., obesity, public health costs), R&D outcomes, compliance with laws and regulations, perceptions of advertising/sponsorships/marketing, social media use, and responses to political/social issues.
- Potential amplification of reputational harm through negative or inaccurate social media commentary.
- Product quality and safety risks, including recalls due to mislabeling, allergens, spoilage, adulteration, or contamination; consequences include direct costs, inventory destruction, lost sales, production and delivery disruptions, legal liabilities (fines, penalties, damages, potential criminal exposure), and lasting damage to brand trust.
- Heightened quality/safety and reputational risks as the company expands into new categories (e.g., nuts, meat convenient foods globally) and distributes alcoholic beverages in the U.S.
- Emphasis on the need for robust oversight of product quality and safety; broader market risk if consumers lose confidence in product integrity industrywide.

nodes.title: Product recalls or other issues or concerns with respect to product quality and safety can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Product recalls or other issues or concerns with respect to product quality and safety can adversely af fect our business.

nodes.summary:
- Consumer demand is highly sensitive to changing preferences, brand image, effectiveness of advertising and digital engagement, and social media perceptions; failure to anticipate trends or invest in data analytics can reduce sales, cause inventory write-offs, and weaken competitiveness. Natural disasters and other disruptions can impair supply, availability, and demand if crisis management is ineffective.
- Reputation and brand image risks stem from ethical, legal, and ESG performance (human rights, DEI, workplace conditions, environment, nutrition), health concerns about products/ingredients, R&D outcomes, product quality and safety issues, regulatory compliance, and reactions to marketing, sponsorships, social media, and sociopolitical events; mismanagement can depress demand.
- Product quality and safety risks, including recalls for mislabeling, allergens, spoilage, or contamination, can drive costs, lost sales, operational disruptions, litigation, penalties, and reputational damage; risks may rise with expansion into nuts, meat convenient foods, and U.S. alcohol distribution. Loss of consumer confidence can extend beyond affected products.
- Competitive pressures from global, regional, private label, and microbrand players—especially The Coca-Cola Company—require strong brand equity, pricing, innovation, distribution, marketing, packaging, and responsiveness to trends. Inability to adopt AI and data analytics or strengthen digital marketing, or to manage supply disruptions and commodity inflation, can erode share and force higher spending.
- Talent risks include attracting, developing, and retaining a diverse, highly skilled workforce (notably in e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics); turnover, labor shortages, or weak succession planning—up to CEO level—can increase costs, drain institutional knowledge, harm results, and damage reputation if DEI progress lags.
- Water scarcity and quality constraints, intensified by climate change and stakeholder scrutiny, threaten supply chains, operations, compliance costs, capital needs (e.g., efficiency technologies), production costs, facility continuity or relocation, achievement of water goals, and reputation.

nodes.title: Any inability to compete effectively can adversely affect our business.
nodes.heading: Any inability to compete ef fectively can adversely af fect our business.
nodes.start_phrase: Our produ cts compete against products of international beverage and convenient food companies that, like us, operate in multiple geographies, as well as regional, local and private label and economy brand manufacturers and other competitors, including smaller companies developing and selling micro brands directly to consumers through e-commerce platforms or through retailers focused on locally sourced products.
nodes.summary:
- Intensifying competition: The company faces strong global, regional, local, private label, and micro-brand rivals (notably The Coca-Cola Company in beverages). Success depends on brand strength, innovation, pricing, quality, variety, distribution, marketing, packaging, convenience, and responsiveness to consumer trends. Risks include failure to promote/innovate products, lagging in AI/data analytics and digital marketing, competitor spending, supply disruptions, and commodity-driven pricing pressure, potentially requiring higher capital and marketing outlays and risking share and sales.
- Talent and diversity risk: Business performance depends on attracting, developing, and retaining a highly skilled and diverse workforce, including expertise in e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics. Unplanned turnover, labor shortages, succession gaps (including at CEO level), and failure to improve diversity can erode institutional knowledge, increase costs, and harm results and reputation.
- Water scarcity risk: Dependence on water for manufacturing and raw material production exposes the company to climate-driven scarcity and stakeholder pressure. Potential impacts include supply chain disruptions, operational constraints, higher compliance and production costs, increased capital investments in water efficiency, facility interruptions or relocations, missed water-use goals, regulatory challenges, and reputational damage.

nodes.title: Failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce can have an adverse effect on our business.
nodes.heading: Failure to attract, develop and maintain a highly skilled and diverse workforce can have an adverse ef fect on our business.

nodes.summary:

Risks include inability to effectively promote existing products, launch new ones, adopt technologies (including AI and data analytics), strengthen digital marketing, respond to supply disruptions and commodity inflation, or match competitors’ spending, potentially requiring higher investments and risking market share and sales.

- Talent and workforce risks: Sustained need to attract, develop, and retain a highly skilled and diverse workforce (including e-commerce, digital marketing, and data analytics capabilities). Risks include unplanned turnover, labor shortages, succession planning challenges (including CEO), loss of institutional knowledge, higher costs due to competition for talent and benefits, and reputational harm if underrepresented communities are not effectively included and advanced.

- Water scarcity and resource dependency: Heavy reliance on water for manufacturing and raw material production exposes the company and partners to risks from water scarcity and climate change. Potential impacts include supply chain disruptions, operational constraints or relocations, increased compliance and capital costs (e.g., water-efficiency technologies), higher production and water costs, failure to meet water-use goals, regulatory and stakeholder pressures, and reputational damage.

nodes.title: Water scarcity can adversely affect our business.
