nodes.heading: Organic r evenue gr owth
nodes.start_phrase:
We define organic revenue growth as a measure that adjusts for the impacts of foreign exchange translation, acquisitions and
divestitures, and where applicable, the impact of an additional week of results every five or six years (53 reporting week),
including in our 2022 financial results.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines PepsiCo’s use of non-GAAP financial measures and emphasizes they are supplemental to U.S. GAAP and may not be comparable across companies.
- Defines “items affecting comparability,” including impacts from new laws/regulations (e.g., tax changes), resolution of tax positions, tax benefits from reorganizations, debt redemptions/tender or exchange offers, non-cash asset impairments, remeasurement of net monetary assets, mark-to-market commodity derivative gains/losses, restructuring and impairment charges under the 2019 Productivity Plan, M&A costs, pension/retiree medical settlement and curtailment gains/losses, debt tender charges, and TCJ Act-related taxes.
- Clarifies pension and retiree medical accounting: service cost, interest cost, expected return on plan assets, and other net periodic costs remain in core results, while settlements/curtailments are treated as items affecting comparability.
- Lists adjusted non-GAAP metrics discussed: cost of sales, gross profit, SG&A, other pension/retiree medical benefits income, net interest expense and other, income tax provision, net income attributable to noncontrolling interests, net income attributable to PepsiCo, operating profit, and diluted EPS—each adjusted for items affecting comparability and also evaluated on a constant-currency basis.
- Describes constant-currency methodology for translating current-year results using prior-year average exchange rates to enhance year-over-year comparability.
- Defines organic revenue growth, excluding the effects of foreign exchange, acquisitions/divestitures, and 53rd-week reporting; notes timing alignment impacts from the Pioneer Foods (AMESA) and Be & Cheery (APAC) acquisitions.
- Defines free cash flow as operating cash flow minus capital spending plus proceeds from sales of property, plant, and equipment; explains its primary uses (acquisitions, debt, dividends, buybacks) and that it is not fully discretionary due to obligations like debt service.
- Defines ROIC and explains its purpose as a capital efficiency metric; introduces net ROIC excluding items affecting comparability, which adjusts for cash and short-term investments, after-tax interest income, and the identified non-comparable items to enable more consistent period-over-period evaluation.
- Provides cross-references to detailed sections: Items Affecting Comparability; Results of Operations – Division Review (Net Revenue and Organic Revenue Growth); and Our Liquidity and Capital Resources (Free Cash Flow and Return on Invested Capital).

nodes.title: Free cash flow
nodes.heading: Free cash flow
nodes.start_phrase:
We define free cash flow as net cash provided by operating activities less capital spending, plus sales of property , plant and
equipment.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on non-GAAP performance metrics used by the company to assess liquidity and capital efficiency.
- Defines Free Cash Flow as net cash from operating activities minus capital spending plus proceeds from sales of property, plant and equipment; emphasizes capital spending as recurring and necessary; notes FCF is primarily used for acquisitions, debt repayments, dividends, and share repurchases; clarifies FCF is not fully discretionary due to non-discretionary obligations; references further detail in “Our Liquidity and Capital Resources.”
- Defines ROIC as net income attributable to PepsiCo plus after-tax interest expense divided by quarterly average debt plus quarterly average common shareholders’ equity; cautions that calculation methods vary across companies; positions ROIC as a measure of capital use and returns.
- Introduces net ROIC excluding items affecting comparability, adjusting ROIC for quarterly average cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments, after-tax interest income, and items affecting comparability; explains this helps evaluate performance consistently across periods and assess capital allocation efficiency; references more detail in “Return on Invested Capital” within “Our Liquidity and Capital Resources.”

nodes.title: Return on invested capital (ROIC) and net ROIC, excluding items affecting comparability
nodes.heading: Return on invested capital (ROIC) and net ROIC, excluding items affecting comparability
nodes.start_phrase:
We define ROIC as net income attribut able to PepsiCo plus interest expense after-tax divided by the sum of quarterly average
debt obligations and quarterly average common shareholders’ equity .
nodes.summary:
- Defines and explains the company’s non-GAAP metric for Free Cash Flow (operating cash flow minus capital spending plus proceeds from PP&E sales), why net capital spending is treated as recurring, how FCF is used (acquisitions, debt repayment, dividends, share repurchases), and that it is not fully discretionary due to obligations like debt service; points to the Liquidity and Capital Resources section for more detail.
- Defines ROIC (net income plus after-tax interest divided by quarterly average debt plus quarterly average equity) and net ROIC excluding items affecting comparability (adjusted for cash and short-term investments, after-tax interest income, and specified non-comparable items); explains their purpose as measures of capital allocation efficiency and comparability across periods, and notes methodologies can differ across companies; references where to find more detail.
- Details “Items Affecting Comparability” and presents GAAP-to-core non-GAAP reconciliations for 2021 and 2020 across key income statement lines (cost of sales, gross profit, SG&A, operating profit, pension/retiree benefits income, net interest expense/other, taxes, noncontrolling interests, and net income attributable to PepsiCo). Adjustment categories include:
  - Mark-to-market impacts
  - Restructuring and impairment charges
  - Acquisition and divestiture-related charges
  - Pension and retiree medical-related impacts
  - Charges related to cash tender offers
  - Tax expense related to the TCJ Act
- Provides diluted EPS reconciliation from GAAP to core non-GAAP for 2021 and 2020, shows the per-share impact of each adjustment, and reports core EPS growth on a constant-currency basis with the effect of foreign exchange translation.
- Includes footnotes noting expected tax on underlying adjustments (by applicable jurisdictions) and rounding considerations.

nodes.title: Items Affecting Comparability
nodes.heading: Items Affecting Comparability
nodes.start_phrase: Our reported financial results in this Form 10-K are impacted by the following items in each of the following years:
nodes.summary:
- Presents “Items Affecting Comparability” with reconciliations from GAAP to Core (non-GAAP) results for 2021 and 2020 across key income statement lines (cost of sales, gross profit, SG&A, operating profit, other pension/retiree medical income, net interest/other, taxes, noncontrolling interests, and net income attributable to PepsiCo).
- Reconciles diluted EPS: GAAP EPS grew 7% (2021 vs. 2020); Core EPS rose 13%, or 12% on a constant-currency basis; shows per‑share impacts of specific adjusting items.
- Details the adjusting items:
  - Mark-to-market net impact from centrally managed commodity derivatives (agricultural, energy, metals), with an explanation of corporate unallocated recording and subsequent division-level reflection to avoid mark-to-market volatility.
  - Restructuring and impairment charges tied to the 2019 multi‑year Productivity Plan.
  - Acquisition and divestiture-related charges (inventory fair value step‑ups, merger/integration, divestiture costs, South Africa socioeconomic program liabilities, employee-related costs, contract terminations, contingent consideration adjustments).
  - Pension and retiree medical-related impacts (settlement charges from lump sums, curtailment gains from plan changes).
  - 2021 charge related to cash tender offers.
  - Tax expense related to the TCJ Act.
- Provides methodology notes: tax effects on adjustments based on applicable jurisdictions; rounding; and foreign exchange translation impact on Core EPS growth.
- Expands on the 2019 Productivity Plan:
  - Objectives: simplify, harmonize, and automate processes; re-engineer go‑to‑market and information systems; optimize manufacturing and supply chain footprint.
  - Program extended through 2026; expected total pre‑tax charges ~$3.15 billion and cash expenditures ~$2.4 billion (revised from ~$2.5 billion and ~$1.6 billion, respectively).
  - Incurred through Dec 25, 2021: ~$1.0 billion pre‑tax, ~$776 million cash.
  - Expected 2022 charges: ~$(350) million pre‑tax and ~$(300) million cash; funded primarily by operating cash flows; majority of remaining costs expected in 2022–2023 with balance through 2026.
- Cross-references to Notes 3 (productivity plan), 13 (acquisitions/divestitures), and 7 (pension/retiree medical) of the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Mark-to-Market Net Impact
nodes.heading: Mark-to-Market Net Impact
nodes.start_phrase: We centrally manage commodity deriv atives on behalf of our divisions.
nodes.summary:
- Explains centralized management of commodity derivatives (agriculture, energy, metals) and mark-to-market accounting for instruments not qualifying for hedge accounting, with gains/losses recorded in corporate unallocated expenses to shield divisional results from volatility until underlying commodity costs are recognized.
- Details the 2019 Multi-Year Productivity Plan: aims to simplify, automate, re-engineer go-to-market and IT systems, and optimize organizational, manufacturing, and supply chain footprints.
- Notes expansion/extension of the plan through 2026 with updated expected pre-tax charges of about $3.15 billion (approx. $2.4 billion cash), up from $2.5 billion ($1.6 billion cash); through Dec 25, 2021, $1.0 billion in pre-tax charges and $776 million cash incurred.
- Projects 2022 charges of roughly $350 million (about $300 million cash), funded primarily by cash from operations; most remaining costs expected in 2022–2023, with the balance through 2026.
- Outlines acquisition and divestiture-related charges, including inventory fair value step-ups, merger/integration and divestiture costs (e.g., South Africa socioeconomic program liabilities, closing and employee costs, contingent consideration gains, contract terminations).
- Summarizes pension and retiree medical impacts, including settlement charges from lump-sum distributions exceeding service/interest costs and curtailment gains from plan changes, with references to related financial statement notes.

nodes.title: Restructuring and Impairment Charges
nodes.heading: Restructuring and Impairment Charges
nodes.start_phrase: The 2019 Productiv ity Plan, publicly announced on February 15, 2019, will leverage new technology and business models to further simplify , harmonize and automate processes; re-engineer our go-to-market and information systems, including deploying the right automation for each market; and simplify our organization and optimize our manufacturing and supply chain footprint.
nodes.summary:
- Explains centralized management of commodity derivatives (agricultural, energy, metals) and mark-to-market accounting for instruments not qualifying for hedge accounting, with gains/losses recorded in corporate unallocated expenses (cost of sales or SG&A) and later reflected in division results when underlying commodity costs are recognized, isolating divisions from mark-to-market volatility.
- Details the 2019 Multi-Year Productivity Plan: aims to simplify, harmonize, automate processes; re-engineer go-to-market and information systems; optimize organization, manufacturing, and supply chain footprint.
- Notes expansion/extension of the plan through 2026, increasing expected pre-tax charges to about $3.15B (from $2.5B) and cash expenditures to about $2.4B (from $1.6B).
- Provides status through Dec 25, 2021: $1.0B pre-tax charges incurred, including $776M cash; 2022 expected charges of ~$350M with ~$300M cash, funded mainly by operating cash; most remaining charges expected in 2022–2023, with balance through 2026. References Note 3.
- Describes acquisition and divestiture-related charges: purchase accounting adjustments (inventory fair value step-up), merger/integration costs, and divestiture costs, including socioeconomic program liabilities in South Africa, closing and employee-related costs, contingent consideration gains, and contract termination/other integration costs. References Note 13.
- Summarizes pension and retiree medical impacts: settlement charges when lump-sum payouts exceed annual service and interest costs, and curtailment gains from plan changes. References Note 7.

nodes.title: Acquisition and Divestiture-Related Charges
nodes.heading: Acquisition and Divestiture-Related Charges
nodes.start_phrase: Acquisition and divestiture-related charges primarily include fair value adjustments to the acquired inventory included in the acquisition-date balance sheets, merger and integration charges and costs associated with divestitures.
nodes.summary:
- Explains mark-to-market treatment for centrally managed commodity derivatives (agricultural, energy, metals): gains/losses recorded in corporate unallocated expenses (cost of sales or SG&A) and later reflected in division results when underlying commodity costs are recognized, insulating divisions from mark-to-market volatility.
- Details the 2019 Productivity Plan to simplify, harmonize, and automate processes; re-engineer go-to-market and IT systems; and optimize organizational, manufacturing, and supply chain footprints; program expanded and extended through 2026.
- Updates financial outlook for the plan: expected total pre-tax charges of approximately $3.15 billion (up from $2.5 billion) and cash expenditures of approximately $2.4 billion (up from $1.6 billion).
- Reports amounts incurred to date through December 25, 2021: $1.0 billion in pre-tax charges and $776 million in cash; 2022 expectation of about $350 million in pre-tax charges and $300 million in cash, funded primarily by cash from operations; majority of remaining costs expected in 2022–2023, with the balance through 2026. References Note 3.
- Outlines acquisition and divestiture-related charges: fair value adjustments to acquired inventory, merger and integration costs, divestiture costs, liabilities for socioeconomic programs in South Africa, closing and employee-related costs, contingent consideration gains, and contract termination costs. References Note 13.
- Summarizes pension and retiree medical-related impacts: settlement charges from lump-sum distributions exceeding annual service and interest costs, and curtailment gains from plan changes. References Note 7.

nodes.title: Pension and Retiree Medical-Related Impact
nodes.heading: Pension and Retiree Medical-Related Impact
nodes.start_phrase: Pension and retiree medical-related impact primarily includes settlement charges related to lump sum distributions exceeding the total of annual service and interest costs, as well as curtailment gains related to plan changes.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of how centrally managed commodity derivatives (agricultural products, energy, metals) are mark-to-market when not hedge-accounted, with gains/losses recorded in corporate unallocated expenses (COGS or SG&A) and later reflected in divisional results when the underlying commodity costs are recognized, insulating divisions from mark-to-market volatility.
- Restructuring and impairment charges focused on the 2019 Productivity Plan: leveraging technology, automation, and organizational/supply chain simplification; program expanded/extended through 2026 with expected pre-tax charges of about $3.15 billion (cash ~$2.4 billion), up from $2.5 billion (cash ~$1.6 billion). Through Dec 25, 2021, incurred ~$1.0 billion pre-tax (cash ~$776 million). For 2022, expected ~$350 million pre-tax (cash ~$300 million), funded primarily by operating cash, with most remaining charges in 2022–2023 and balance through 2026. See Note 3.
- Acquisition and divestiture-related charges including acquired inventory fair value step-ups, merger/integration costs, divestiture costs, and items such as liabilities for socioeconomic programs in South Africa, closing and employee-related costs, gains on contingent consideration, and contract termination costs. See Note 13.
- Pension and retiree medical impacts including settlement charges from lump-sum distributions and curtailment gains from plan changes. See Note 7.
- Charges from cash tender offers for long-term debt, consisting of premiums paid over carrying value and losses on treasury rate locks used to hedge interest rate risk. See Note 8.
- Tax expense related to the TCJ Act reflecting adjustments to the mandatory transition tax liability. See Note 5.

nodes.title: Charge Related to Cash Tender Offers
nodes.heading: Charge Related to Cash T ender Of fers
nodes.start_phrase: As a result of the cash tender offers for some of our long-term debt, we recorde d a charge primarily representing the tender price paid over the carryin g value of the tendered notes and loss on treasury rate locks used to mitigate the interest rate risk on the cash tender of fers.
nodes.summary:
- Summarizes charges from cash tender offers on long-term debt, primarily the premium paid over carrying value of tendered notes and losses on treasury rate locks used to hedge interest rate risk; references Note 8 for details.
- Outlines tax expense related to the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA), specifically adjustments to the mandatory transition tax liability; references Note 5 for details.

nodes.title: Tax Expense Related to the TCJ Act
nodes.heading: Tax Expense Related to the TCJ Act
nodes.start_phrase: Tax expense related to the TCJ Act reflects adjustments to the mandatory transition tax liability under the TCJ Act.
nodes.summary:
- Records a charge from cash tender offers for long-term debt, reflecting premiums paid over carrying value and losses on treasury rate locks (see Note 8).
- Recognizes tax expense adjustments related to the TCJ Act’s mandatory transition tax (see Note 5).
- Outlines liquidity and capital resources: sufficient liquidity from operations, approximately $3.5 billion pre-tax proceeds from the Juice Transaction, commercial paper, long-term debt, and cash/cash equivalents to fund debt service, acquisitions (including Pioneer Foods–related programs in South Africa), leases, contractual commitments, capital expenditures, TCJ Act transition tax, dividends, and share repurchases; no material guarantees or off-balance sheet financing.
- States COVID-19 did not materially impact sources/uses of cash and is not expected to materially affect future liquidity; continued monitoring (see Risk Factors and Note 1).
- Notes that as of December 25, 2021, cash subject to currency controls/restrictions was not material.
- Details TCJ Act transition tax: imposed on undistributed international earnings (including $18.9 billion held abroad as of December 30, 2017); remaining liability $2.9 billion as of December 25, 2021, payable through 2026, with approximately $309 million expected in 2022; future IRS guidance may affect recorded amounts (see Note 5).
- Describes supplier payment practices and supply chain finance: typical payment terms of 60–90 days; voluntary supplier participation in bank-led receivables financing leveraging PepsiCo’s credit; PepsiCo is not a party, provides no guarantees, has no economic interest in participation decisions, and supplier obligations/terms remain unchanged.

nodes.title: Our Liquidity and Capital Resources
nodes.heading: Our Liquidity and Capital Resour ces
nodes.start_phrase: We believe that our cash generating capability and financial condition, together with our revolving credit facilities, working capital lines and other available methods of debt financing, such as commercial paper borrowings and long-term debt financing,
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Liquidity and Capital Resources, asserting sufficient liquidity from operating cash flows, revolving credit facilities, working capital lines, commercial paper, long-term debt, and cash/equivalents to fund operating, investing, and financing needs, including capital spending.
- Primary liquidity sources include operating cash, approximately $3.5 billion pre-tax proceeds from the Juice Transaction, commercial paper and long-term debt issuances, and cash/equivalents.
- Uses of cash cover debt and interest payments; acquisitions (including socioeconomic program support in South Africa tied to the Pioneer Foods acquisition); operating leases; purchase, marketing, and other contractual commitments; capital expenditures; TCJ Act transition tax payments; dividends; and share repurchases.
- No guarantees or off-balance sheet financing arrangements (including variable interest entities) expected to materially impact liquidity; references to Risk Factors and related notes.
- COVID-19 impact on liquidity has not been material to date and is not expected to be material going forward; continued monitoring noted.
- Cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments subject to currency controls or exchange restrictions were not material as of December 25, 2021.
- TCJ Act: one-time mandatory transition tax on undistributed international earnings; remaining liability of $2.9 billion as of December 25, 2021, payable through 2026, with about $309 million expected in 2022; amounts may change with future IRS guidance.
- Supplier payment terms generally 60–90 days; maintenance of voluntary supply chain finance programs with global financial institutions. Participation is supplier-driven; PepsiCo is not a party, provides no guarantees, and obligations/payment terms are unchanged. Outstanding payables under these programs were $1.5 billion (2021) and $1.2 billion (2020); no material impact on liquidity expected.
- Seasonality affects working capital (sales generally highest in Q3 and lowest in Q1).
- Ongoing evaluation of transactions to enhance shareholder value (acquisitions, divestitures, joint ventures, dividends, share repurchases, productivity/efficiency initiatives), which may generate future cash inflows or outflows.
- Cash flow summary:
  - 2021 operating cash flow: $11.6 billion (up from $10.6 billion in 2020), driven by favorable working capital and operating profit, partly offset by higher pension/retiree medical contributions and higher cash taxes.
  - 2021 investing cash use: $3.3 billion, primarily net capital spending of $4.5 billion, partly offset by $1.1 billion of maturities of short-term investments.
  - 2020 investing cash use: $11.6 billion, mainly acquisitions (Rockstar $3.85 billion, Pioneer Foods $1.2 billion, Be & Cheery $0.7 billion), net capital spending of $4.2 billion, and $1.1 billion of short-term investment purchases.
  - The company continues to review capital spending plans and believes liquidity is sufficient to meet these needs.
  - 2021 financing cash use: $10.8 billion, primarily dividends of $5.8 billion, cash tender offers/debt redemptions of $4.8 billion, and $3.5 billion in long-term debt repayments.

nodes.title: Operating Activities
nodes.heading: Operating Activities
nodes.start_phrase: In 2021, net cash provided by operating activities was $11.6 billion, compared to $10.6 billion in the prior year.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of supplier financing arrangements: amounts owed to suppliers participating in supply chain finance are recorded in accounts payable and other current liabilities; outstanding balances were $1.5B (2021) and $1.2B (2020). These arrangements did not materially affect liquidity or capital resources and are not expected to in the foreseeable future.
- Seasonality effects: working capital and operating cash flows are seasonally impacted, with sales highest in Q3 and lowest in Q1.
- Ongoing capital allocation strategies: the company regularly evaluates acquisitions, divestitures, joint ventures, dividends, share repurchases, productivity/efficiency initiatives, and other structural changes that may generate or use cash.
- Cash flow summary (2021 vs. 2020):
  - Operating activities: $11.6B vs. $10.6B; increase driven by favorable working capital and operating profit, partially offset by higher pension/retiree medical contributions and higher cash taxes.
  - Investing activities: $(3.3)B vs. $(11.6)B; 2021 driven by net capital spending of $4.5B offset by $1.1B of maturities of >3-month investments; 2020 driven by acquisitions (Rockstar $3.85B, Pioneer Foods $1.2B, Be & Cheery $0.7B), net capital spending of $4.2B, and purchases of >3-month investments of $1.1B.
  - Financing activities: $(10.8)B vs. $3.8B; 2021 primarily due to $5.8B dividends, $4.8B cash tender offers/debt redemptions, and $3.5B payments of long-term debt.
- Liquidity and capital spending: the company regularly reviews capital spending plans amid COVID-19 uncertainty and believes liquidity is sufficient to meet capital needs.
- Cross-references: notes to consolidated financial statements for details on capital spending (Note 1), investments in debt securities (Note 9), and acquisitions (Note 13).

nodes.title: Investing Activities
nodes.heading: Investing Activities
nodes.start_phrase: In 2021, net cash used for investing activities was $3.3 billion, primarily reflec ting net capital spending of $4.5 billion, partially offset by maturities of short-term investments with maturities greater than three months of $1.1 billion.
nodes.summary:
- Disclosure on supplier financing (supply chain finance): amounts recorded in accounts payable/other current liabilities; outstanding balances of $1.5 billion (Dec 25, 2021) and $1.2 billion (Dec 26, 2020); arrangements not material to liquidity or capital resources and not expected to be material going forward.
- Seasonality: working capital and weekly sales are seasonal—strongest in Q3 due to holidays, weakest in Q1.
- Strategic cash uses/sources under consideration: acquisitions, divestitures, joint ventures, dividends, share repurchases, productivity/efficiency initiatives, and other structural actions that could drive future cash inflows/outflows.
- Consolidated cash flow summary:
  - 2021 vs. 2020: Operating cash flow $11.6B vs. $10.6B; Investing cash flow $(3.3)B vs. $(11.6)B; Financing cash flow $(10.8)B vs. $3.8B.
- Operating activities: 2021 increase driven by favorable working capital and operating profit; partially offset by higher pre-tax pension/retiree medical contributions and higher cash tax payments.
- Investing activities:
  - 2021: Net use of $3.3B, mainly net capital spending of $4.5B, partly offset by $1.1B maturities of short-term investments (>3 months).
  - 2020: Net use of $11.6B, driven by acquisitions (Rockstar $3.85B, Pioneer Foods $1.2B, Be & Cheery $0.7B), net capital spending of $4.2B, and $1.1B purchases of >3-month investments.
  - References to notes for capital spending by division, debt securities investments, and acquisitions.
- Capital spending outlook: plans reviewed regularly amid COVID-19 uncertainty; sufficient liquidity to meet net capital spending needs.
- Financing activities (2021): Net use of $10.8B, primarily dividends of $5.8B, cash tender offers/debt redemption of $4.8B, and $3.5B repayments of long-term debt.

nodes.title: Financing Activities
nodes.heading: Financing Activities
nodes.start_phrase: In 2021, net cash used for financing activities was $10.8 billion, primarily reflecting the return of operating cash flow to our shareholders largely through dividend payments of $5.8 billion, cash tender offers/debt redemption of $4.8 billion, payments of long-term debt borrowings of $3.5 billion and payments of acquisition-related contingent consideration of $0.8 billion, partiall y offset by proceeds from issuances of long-term debt of $4.1 billion.
nodes.summary:
- Supply chain finance arrangements: Accounts payable to suppliers in these programs recorded in current liabilities; $1.5B outstanding at Dec 25, 2021 and $1.2B at Dec 26, 2020; no material impact on liquidity or capital resources expected.
- Seasonality: Working capital needs vary with sales patterns—highest in Q3, lowest in Q1.
- Strategic actions: Ongoing evaluation of acquisitions, divestitures, JVs, dividends, share repurchases, productivity and efficiency initiatives, which may affect future cash flows.
- Cash flow summary (2021 vs 2020): Operating $11.6B vs $10.6B; Investing $(3.3)B vs $(11.6)B; Financing $(10.8)B vs $3.8B.
- Operating activities: 2021 increase driven by favorable working capital and profit, partially offset by higher pension/retiree medical contributions and higher cash taxes.
- Investing activities: 2021 primarily net capital spending of $4.5B offset by $1.1B maturities of short-term investments. 2020 driven by acquisitions (Rockstar $3.85B, Pioneer Foods $1.2B, Be & Cheery $0.7B), capex $4.2B, and $1.1B purchases of short-term investments. Company asserts sufficient liquidity for capex amid COVID-19 uncertainty.
- Financing activities: 2021 outflows from dividends ($5.8B), debt redemption/tenders ($4.8B), long-term debt repayments ($3.5B), acquisition-related contingent consideration ($0.8B), partly offset by $4.1B in long-term debt issuance. 2020 inflows from $13.8B long-term debt issuance offset by dividends and buybacks ($7.5B), long-term debt repayments ($1.8B), and redemptions ($1.1B).
- Capital structure and shareholder returns: 2018 $15B repurchase program expired June 30, 2021; 2022 repurchase program announced. Dividend increased 7% to $4.60 per share; plan to return ~$7.7B to shareholders in 2022 ($6.2B dividends, $1.5B buybacks).
- Free cash flow (non-GAAP): 2021 $7.16B vs 2020 $6.43B; used for acquisitions and financing (debt, dividends, repurchases). Commitment to maintain Tier 1 commercial paper access.
- Credit rating considerations: Downgrades could raise borrowing costs and limit market access, particularly in commercial paper; cross-references to Risk Factors and debt notes.
- Cross-references: Additional details in notes on capital spending, investments in debt securities, acquisitions, and debt obligations; material changes in income statement items discussed in Results of Operations and Items Affecting Comparability.

nodes.title: Free Cash Flow
nodes.heading: Free Cash Flow
nodes.start_phrase: The table below reconciles net cash provided by operating activities, as reflected on our cash flow statement, to our free cash flow.
nodes.summary:
- Financing activities: Notes payments of $0.8 billion for acquisition-related contingent consideration, partially offset by $4.1 billion of long-term debt issuances. For 2020, net cash provided by financing activities was $3.8 billion, driven by $13.8 billion of long-term debt issuances, offset by $7.5 billion in dividends and share repurchases, $1.8 billion in debt repayments, and $1.1 billion in redemptions. References to Note 8 for debt obligations.
- Capital structure and shareholder returns: Company annually reviews capital structure, dividend policy, and repurchases with the Board. 2018 share repurchase program authorized up to $15.0 billion (July 1, 2018–June 30, 2021). A new 2022 share repurchase program was announced. Dividend increased 7% to $4.60 per share effective with the expected June 2022 payment. Planned 2022 shareholder returns total ~$7.7 billion ($6.2 billion dividends; $1.5 billion repurchases). References to Item 5 for details.
- Free cash flow (non-GAAP): Reconciles 2021 vs. 2020—net cash from operating activities $11,616 million vs. $10,613 million (+9%); capital spending $(4,625) million vs. $(4,240) million; sales of PP&E $166 million vs. $55 million; free cash flow $7,157 million vs. $6,428 million (+11%). Free cash flow is used for acquisitions, debt repayments, dividends, and share repurchases.
- Liquidity and credit ratings: Intends to maintain Tier 1 commercial paper access for financial flexibility and favorable market access. Warns that credit rating downgrades—especially below investment grade—could raise borrowing costs and limit access to capital/credit markets; downgrades of short-term ratings could restrict commercial paper market access, necessitating more expensive financing. References to Item 1A, Business Risks, and Note 8.
- Cross-references: Material changes in income statement line items are addressed in “Results of Operations – Division Review” and “Items Affecting Comparability.”

nodes.title: Material Changes in Line Items in Our Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.heading: Material Changes in Line Items in Our Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.start_phrase: Material changes in line items in our consolidated statement of cash flows are discussed in “Our Liquidity and Capital Resources.”
nodes.summary:
- Overview of financing activities: 2021 included $0.8B in acquisition-related contingent consideration payments, partially offset by $4.1B of long-term debt issuance; 2020 provided $3.8B net cash from financing, driven by $13.8B of long-term debt issuances offset by $7.5B in dividends and share repurchases, $1.8B in debt repayments, and $1.1B in redemptions.
- Capital allocation and shareholder returns: Regular Board review of capital structure; 2018 $15B repurchase program concluded in June 2021; new 2022 repurchase program announced; 7% dividend increase to $4.60/share effective June 2022; plan to return ~$7.7B to shareholders in 2022 ($6.2B dividends, $1.5B repurchases).
- Free cash flow (non-GAAP): Reconciliation from operating cash flow shows FCF increased 11% to $7.2B in 2021 (from $6.4B in 2020); primary uses are acquisitions, debt, dividends, and buybacks; intent to maintain Tier 1 commercial paper access and financial flexibility.
- Liquidity and credit considerations: Discussion of risks from potential credit rating downgrades affecting borrowing costs and market access; references to Risk Factors and notes for details.
- Material changes in financial statements:
  - Balance sheet: Total assets declined slightly to $92.4B (from $92.9B), driven by lower cash and short-term investments, increases in assets held for sale and PP&E, and lower other indefinite-lived intangibles; total liabilities decreased to $76.2B (from $79.4B) due to lower long-term debt and other liabilities, partially offset by higher current liabilities and liabilities held for sale; notes cite impacts from pensions/retiree medical, Rockstar contingent consideration, and leases.
  - Income statement and cash flow statement changes referenced to other sections.
  - Equity changes referred to the consolidated statement of equity.
- Return on Invested Capital (non-GAAP): ROIC improved to 16.0% in 2021 from 14.7% in 2020, with supporting metrics for net income, interest expense (net of tax), and average invested capital.

nodes.title: OUR CRITICAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES AND ESTIMATES
nodes.heading: OUR CRITICAL ACCOUNTING POLICIES AND ESTIMA TES
nodes.start_phrase: An appreciation of our critical accounting policies and estimates is necessary to understand our financial results.
nodes.summary:
- Reconciliation of ROIC to Core Net ROIC (non-GAAP) for 2021 and 2020, detailing adjustments for:
  - Average cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments
  - Interest income and related tax
  - Mark-to-market net impact
  - Restructuring and impairment charges
  - Acquisition and divestiture-related charges
  - Pension and retiree medical-related impacts
  - Tax expense related to the TCJ Act
  - Other net tax benefits
  Result: ROIC of 16.0% (2021) and 14.7% (2020) reconciled to Core Net ROIC of 18.4% (2021) and 19.9% (2020).

- Overview of critical accounting policies and estimates, emphasizing management judgment, potential impacts from COVID-19, consistent application, and Audit Committee oversight. Key areas:
  - Revenue recognition
  - Goodwill and other intangible assets
  - Income tax expense and accruals
  - Pension and retiree medical plans

- Revenue recognition policy:
  - Revenue recognized upon shipment or delivery when control transfers for beverage and convenient food products.
  - Generally no right of return; however, DSD (including certain chilled) and some warehouse products are replaced if damaged or out-of-date; reserves recorded for anticipated returns/damages.
  - Sales on cash or credit terms (typically 30 days in the U.S., 30–90 days internationally) with possible early payment discounts.
  - Expected credit losses estimated using historical experience (past dues, write-offs, aging), customer data, and forward-looking information, including global economic uncertainty.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition
nodes.heading: Revenue Recognition
nodes.start_phrase: We recognize revenue when our performance obligation is satisfied.
nodes.summary:
- Presents a reconciliation of ROIC to Core Net ROIC (non-GAAP) for 2021 and 2020. ROIC was 16.0% (2021) and 14.7% (2020); after adjustments, Core Net ROIC was 18.4% (2021) and 19.9% (2020). Key reconciling items include the impact of average cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments (2.2 pts in 2021; 3.4 pts in 2020), interest income, related taxes, mark-to-market effects, restructuring and impairment charges, acquisition/divestiture-related items, pension and retiree medical impacts, TCJ Act-related tax expense, and other net tax benefits.
- Outlines “Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates,” emphasizing their significance, the role of management judgment, consistency of application, COVID-19-related uncertainties, and Audit Committee oversight. The listed critical areas are: revenue recognition; goodwill and other intangible assets; income tax expense and accruals; and pension and retiree medical plans.
- Details revenue recognition:
  - Revenue recognized upon shipment or delivery when control transfers; typical terms preclude returns.
  - Company policies replace damaged/out-of-date products in DSD and certain warehouse channels; reserves are recorded based on estimates.
  - Credit sales generally require payment within 30 days in the U.S. and 30–90 days internationally; expected credit losses are estimated using historical experience, customer data, aging, and forward-looking factors, including COVID-19 effects.
  - Practices to ensure freshness and manage shipment quantities include DSD shelf placement and monitoring customer inventory levels.
  - Marketplace spending (sales incentives/discounts) is primarily recorded as a reduction of revenue and includes payments for in-store displays, shelf space, new product distribution, price promotions, and support for independent bottlers’ marketing.
  - Many incentives are based on annual targets; accruals are recognized as products are delivered, using historical experience and management judgment, with true-ups recognized when determined. Advertising/marketing costs tied to annual targets are recognized as incurred. Reference is made to Note 2 for further details.
- Describes accounting for goodwill and other intangible assets:
  - Brand development costs are expensed as incurred; acquired brands/intangibles are recognized at fair value in business combinations with any excess consideration recorded as goodwill.
  - Fair value determinations require significant estimates and assumptions (including COVID-19 impacts), considering market participants, product life cycles, market share, consumer awareness, brand history, future cash flows, and discount rates.
  - Criteria for indefinite-lived brands include strong historical performance and intent/ability to support with ongoing marketplace spending; otherwise, brands are amortized over 20–40 years. Useful lives are based on factors such as market share, brand awareness/history, expansion prospects, regulatory constraints, and macroeconomic conditions.
  - Notes prior acquisitions that included reacquired franchise rights with exclusive, perpetual manufacturing/distribution privileges; factors in determining useful life are introduced (discussion truncated).

nodes.title: Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets
nodes.heading: Goodwill and Other Intangible Assets
nodes.start_phrase: We sell products under a number of brand names, many of which were develop ed by us.
nodes.summary:
- Sales and distribution practices: commitment to product freshness, DSD shelf placement by company employees, customer shelf/storage constraints regulating shipment quantities, and inventory monitoring across distribution channels; inclusion of COVID‑19-related estimates for customer creditworthiness, default, and recovery.
- Revenue recognition and marketplace spending: sales incentives/discounts (e.g., in-store displays, new product distribution, shelf space, price promotions) recorded as revenue reductions; support for independent bottlers; accruals for annual-target programs (bottler funding, volume rebates) based on contracts and historical experience; recognition of advertising/marketing costs; references to Note 2.
- Goodwill and intangible assets: brand development expensed as incurred; acquisition accounting assigns fair value to identifiable intangibles with excess as goodwill; significant fair value assumptions (including COVID‑19 impacts) around market dynamics, cash flows, and discount rates; criteria for indefinite-lived brands vs. amortizable brands (typically 20–40 years).
- Franchise rights: evaluation of reacquired bottling/franchise rights for indefinite life based on perpetual arrangements and absence of limiting factors; finite-lived rights amortized over remaining contractual terms.
- Impairment testing: annual (Q3) or more frequent assessments of indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill using qualitative then, if needed, quantitative DCF analyses (growth, perpetuity, WACC) tied to market data and internal plans; potential adverse impact from macro, competitive, and COVID‑19 factors; amortizable intangibles tested upon significant environmental changes and written down if impaired; references to Notes 2 and 4 and Risk Factors.
- Income taxes: determination of annual effective tax rate based on income, statutory rates, structure, and transfer pricing; judgment in uncertain tax positions with reserves and interest adjusted as circumstances evolve (audits, law changes, settlements); application of estimated annual effective tax rate to quarterly results, with separate treatment for significant or unusual items; reference to Risk Factors.

nodes.title: Income Tax Expense and Accruals
nodes.heading: Income T ax Expense and Accruals
nodes.start_phrase: Our annual tax rate is based on our income, statutory tax rates and tax structure and transactions, including transfer pricing arrangements, available to us in the various jurisdictions in which we operate.
nodes.summary:
- Intangible assets: Certain franchise rights are classified as indefinite-lived due to perpetual bottling arrangements and absence of limiting legal, regulatory, contractual, competitive, or economic factors; other franchise rights are amortized over remaining contractual terms.
- Impairment testing: Indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill are tested at least annually (or more frequently) using a qualitative screen and, if needed, a quantitative discounted cash flow approach. Key inputs include projected cash flows, sales growth, perpetuity growth, and WACC, with consideration of macroeconomic and COVID-19 impacts. Amortizable intangibles are tested upon significant operational or macro changes; impairment is recognized if undiscounted cash flows don’t recover carrying value.
- Income taxes: The annual effective tax rate is driven by income, statutory rates, tax structure (including transfer pricing), and significant judgment around uncertain tax positions with reserves adjusted as facts change. Quarterly results apply an estimated annual rate, with separate computation for significant or unusual items (including prior-year resolutions). Differences between book and cash taxes create deferred tax assets/liabilities; valuation allowances are recorded when realization is not more likely than not. Reported ETR was 21.8% in 2021 vs 20.9% in 2020.
- Pension and retiree medical: U.S. and certain international employees participate in pension plans; some U.S. and Canada retirees receive capped, partially subsidized medical/life benefits with subsidies being phased out. Expense is based on service cost, interest cost, expected return on assets, and other gains/losses.
- Key actuarial assumptions: Employee demographics (turnover, retirement age, mortality), expected asset returns, spot-rate yield curves for service/interest cost and liability valuation, salary growth for earnings-based plans, and health care cost trend rates.
- Cross-references: Notes to the consolidated financial statements and Risk Factors are cited for additional detail.

nodes.title: Pension and Retiree Medical Plans
nodes.heading: Pension and Retir ee Medical Plans
nodes.start_phrase: Our pension plans cover certain employees in the United States and certain international employees.
nodes.summary:
- Describes how the company’s effective tax rate differs from its cash tax rate due to permanent and temporary differences, with temporary differences creating deferred tax assets and liabilities and potential valuation allowances.
- Notes that tax adjustments from the resolution of prior-year tax matters are treated as discrete items.
- Reports the annual effective tax rate: 21.8% in 2021 versus 20.9% in 2020, and references related financial statement notes.
- Outlines the company’s pension and retiree medical plans: coverage for certain U.S. and international employees, benefit formulas based on service and/or earnings, retiree medical and life insurance eligibility, employer cost caps with retiree contributions, and the phasing out of certain retiree medical subsidies.
- Identifies the components of annual pension and retiree medical expense: service cost, interest cost, other gains/losses, and expected return on assets.
- Lists key assumptions used in measurement: employee demographics (turnover, retirement age, mortality), expected return on plan assets, yield-curve spot rates for service/interest cost and liability valuation, salary growth rates for pay-based pension plans, and healthcare cost trend rates for retiree medical.

nodes.title: Our Assumptions
nodes.heading: Our Assumptions
nodes.start_phrase: The determination of pension and retiree medical expenses and obligations requires the use of assumptions to estimate the amount of benefits that employees earn while working, as well as the present value of those benefits.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the difference between the financial statement effective tax rate and the cash tax rate, noting permanent vs. temporary differences that create deferred tax assets and liabilities, and the use of valuation allowances when realization is not more likely than not.
- Notes treatment of tax adjustments from resolutions of prior-year matters as discrete items and reports the annual tax rate: 21.8% in 2021 vs. 20.9% in 2020, with references to “Other Consolidated Results” and Note 5.
- Describes the company’s pension and retiree medical plans: who is covered, benefit determination (service years and/or earnings), caps on the company’s share of retiree medical costs, and phased reduction of certain retiree medical subsidies; references “Items Affecting Comparability” and Note 7.
- Details how pension and retiree medical expense is measured: key components (service cost, interest cost, expected return on assets, and other gains/losses) and significant assumptions (demographics, expected asset returns, yield-curve spot rates/discount rates, salary growth for earnings-based plans, and health care cost trend rates).
- Discusses the use of high-quality long-term corporate bond yields—specifically the Mercer Above Mean Curve—to set discount rates aligned with expected benefit payments, and notes annual review of actuarial assumptions and long-term return expectations.
- Outlines the process for setting health care trend rates, considering claims experience, plan design, technology, carrier changes, and demographics.
- Provides weighted-average assumptions for 2020–2022 for pension and retiree medical (service and interest cost discount rates, expected return on assets, salary growth, and current health care cost trend), indicating higher discount rates in 2022 and expected returns around 6% (pension) and ~5.5% (retiree medical).
- States the outlook that total pension and retiree medical expense is expected to decrease in 2022 due to plan changes and higher discount rates.
- Presents sensitivity analysis: a 25-basis-point decrease in discount rates would increase 2022 pre-tax pension and retiree medical expense by $37, and a 25-basis-point decrease in expected return on assets would increase expense by $49.

nodes.title: Sensitivity of Assumptions
nodes.heading: Sensitivity of Assumptions
nodes.start_phrase: A decrease in each of the collective discount rates or in the expected rate of return assumptions would increase expense for our benefit plans.
nodes.summary:
- Focuses on pension and retiree medical plan accounting assumptions, their review process, and impact on expenses and obligations.
- Discount rates are set each measurement date using high-quality long-term corporate bond yields, specifically the Mercer Above Mean Curve to match benefit payment timing and amounts.
- Actuarial assumptions (including expected returns and health care trend rates) are reviewed annually; interim remeasurements occur for significant events. Short-term asset returns do not drive changes in long-term expected return assumptions.
- Health care cost trend rates are based on claims experience, inputs from health plans/actuaries, industry knowledge, demographics, plan design, new technologies, and carrier changes.
- Provides weighted-average assumptions for 2020–2022 for pension and retiree medical plans (service and interest cost discount rates, expected returns on plan assets, salary increases, and current health care trend rates).
- Management expects total pension and retiree medical expense to decrease in 2022 due to plan changes and higher discount rates.
- Sensitivity analysis: a 25 bp decrease in discount rates would increase 2022 pre-tax expense by $37; a 25 bp decrease in expected return would increase expense by $49.
- Funding policy: contribute to pension trusts when tax-deductible; retiree medical plans generally funded on a pay-as-you-go basis, with periodic reviews for additional funding options.
- Discretionary U.S. defined benefit plan contributions of $75 million made in January 2022 and an additional $75 million expected in Q3 2022.
- Notes that contributions can change due to interest rates, asset returns, and legal changes; ongoing monitoring of COVID-19 impacts and evaluation of de-risking strategies; cross-references Note 7 for more detail on assumptions, investment strategy, contributions, and future benefit payments.

nodes.title: Funding
nodes.heading: Funding
nodes.start_phrase: We make contributions to pension trusts that provide plan benefits for certain pension plans.
nodes.summary:
- Funding of pension and retiree medical plans: policy to contribute in line with tax efficiency; retiree medical largely pay‑as‑you‑go; discretionary U.S. pension contributions of $75 million in January 2022 with an additional $75 million expected in Q3 2022; contributions may change due to interest rates, asset returns, and laws; ongoing monitoring of COVID‑19 impacts and risk‑reduction strategies.

- Consolidated financial results (2019–2021):
  - Income statement: Net revenue grew to $79.5B in 2021; operating profit $11.2B; net income attributable to PepsiCo $7.6B; diluted EPS $5.49; notable swing to other pension/retiree medical income in 2021.
  - Comprehensive income: OCI driven by currency translation losses, cash flow hedge gains, and pension/retiree medical adjustments; 2021 comprehensive income attributable to PepsiCo $8.2B.
  - Cash flows: Strong operating cash flow ($11.6B in 2021); significant capital spending; lower net investing outflows vs. 2020; financing included debt issuance/repayment, dividends (~$5.8B), limited share repurchases in 2021.
  - Balance sheet (12/25/21): Total assets $92.4B; cash and equivalents $5.6B; goodwill and other intangibles significant; total liabilities $76.2B; long‑term debt $36.0B; total equity $16.2B.
  - Statement of equity: Movements in retained earnings, AOCI, share‑based compensation, repurchases, and dividends (cash dividends declared per share $4.2475 in 2021).

- Basis of presentation and key policies (U.S. GAAP):
  - Consolidation, equity method, exclusion of Venezuelan subsidiaries due to restrictions.
  - Classification of costs between cost of sales and SG&A; use of estimates with added uncertainty from COVID‑19.
  - Fiscal calendar (last Saturday of December; 53‑week year in 2022); international operations moved to monthly calendar in Q4 2021.

- Segment reporting:
  - Seven reportable segments: FLNA, QFNA, PBNA, LatAm, Europe, AMESA, APAC; global footprint across 200+ countries.
  - Allocation methodologies for share‑based compensation, pension/retiree medical service costs, and centrally managed commodity derivatives.
  - Segment performance (2019–2021): Net revenue and operating profit by division; increases reflecting acquisitions (Pioneer Foods, Be & Cheery).
  - Revenue mix: Approximate beverage vs. convenient foods contribution by international regions; consolidated about 45% beverage/55% convenient foods; Walmart ~13% of consolidated net revenue.
  - COVID‑19 related 2020–2021 charges/credits by division (credit losses, customer payments, inventory, employee compensation/protection, and other).

- Other division information:
  - Total assets and capital spending by division; corporate assets driven by cash/short‑term investments and other central items.
  - Amortization of intangibles and depreciation by division.
  - Net revenue and long‑lived assets by country (notably U.S., Mexico, Russia, Canada, China, U.K., South Africa).

- Significant accounting policies (Note 2):
  - Revenue recognition upon shipment/delivery; handling of merchandising activities and product returns; reserves for damaged/out‑of‑date products.
  - Credit terms and expected credit loss methodology; monitoring of concentration risk.
  - Total marketplace spending: sales incentives/discounts, bottler funding, and advertising; timing, accruals, and upfront customer payments.
  - Advertising and marketing spend levels and deferrals; distribution costs in SG&A.
  - Software capitalization and amortization.
  - Commitments/contingencies recognition.
  - R&D expense levels and classification.
  - Goodwill and indefinite‑lived intangible impairment testing approach and assumptions; treatment of amortizable intangibles.
  - Other policies: cash equivalents, inventories (FIFO/LIFO/average), PP&E depreciation, foreign currency translation.

- Recently adopted accounting guidance: 2021 adoption of FASB income tax simplification; no material impact.

- Restructuring and impairment (Note 3):
  - 2019 multi‑year productivity plan expanded and extended through 2026.
  - Expected pre‑tax charges increased to ~$3.15B (cash ~$2.4B): ~55% severance/employee costs, 10% non‑cash asset impairments, 35% other implementation costs.
  - Expected charge allocation across divisions and corporate.

structure.title: Recently Issued Accounting Pronouncements - Adopted
structure.heading: Recently Issued Accounting Pronouncements - Adopted
structure.start_phrase: In 2019, the Financ ial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) issued guidance to simplify the accounting for income taxes.
structure.summary:
- Summary of key accounting policies and notes referenced in the table of contents:
  - Pension, retiree medical, and savings plans (Note 7).
  - Financial instruments (Note 9).
  - Cash equivalents defined as highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less.
  - Inventories (Note 14) measured at lower of cost or net realizable value using average, FIFO, or limited LIFO.
  - Property, plant and equipment (Note 14) recorded at historical cost; straight-line depreciation over useful lives; construction in progress not depreciated until placed in service.
  - Translation of foreign subsidiaries: assets/liabilities at period-end rates, revenues/expenses at average rates; cumulative translation adjustments recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss.

- Recently adopted accounting guidance:
  - 2019 FASB simplification of income tax accounting addressing equity method transitions, tax basis step-ups in goodwill, recognition of tax law changes in the period of enactment (including estimated annual tax rate updates), and classification for hybrid tax regimes.
  - Adopted in Q1 2021 with no material impact on consolidated financial statements or disclosures.

- Restructuring and impairment charges (Note 3) – 2019 Multi-Year Productivity Plan:
  - Objectives: simplify, harmonize, and automate processes; re-engineer go-to-market and IT; tailor automation by market; streamline organization; optimize manufacturing and supply chain footprint.
  - Plan expanded and extended through end of 2026.
  - Updated expected pre-tax charges of approximately $3.15 billion (previously $2.5 billion), including about $2.4 billion cash expenditures (previously $1.6 billion).
  - Cost composition: ~55% severance/employee-related, ~10% non-cash asset impairments from plant closures, ~35% other implementation costs.
  - Expected pre-tax charge allocation by division: FLNA 15%, QFNA 1%, PBNA 25%, LatAm 10%, Europe 25%, AMESA 5%, APAC 4%, Corporate 15%.

structure.title: Restructuring and Impairment Charges
structure.heading: Note 3 — Restructuring and Impairment Charges
structure.start_phrase: The 2019 Productiv ity Plan, publicly announced on February 15, 2019, will leverage new technology and business models to further simplify , harmonize and automate processes; re-engineer our go-to-market and information systems, including deploying the right automation for each market; and simplify our organization and optimize our manufacturing and supply chain footprint.
structure.summary:
- Overview of accounting policies and Table of Contents references:
  - Pension, Retiree Medical and Savings Plans (Note 7) and Financial Instruments (Note 9).
  - Cash equivalents defined as highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less.
  - Inventories valued at lower of cost or net realizable value using average cost, FIFO, or limited LIFO.
  - Property, plant and equipment recorded at historical cost; straight-line depreciation; construction in progress not depreciated until placed in service.
  - Foreign subsidiaries’ financial statements translated using period-end rates for assets/liabilities and average rates for income/expenses; currency translation adjustments recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss.

- Recently adopted accounting pronouncements:
  - Adoption (Q1 2021) of FASB’s 2019 guidance simplifying income tax accounting (equity method transition deferred taxes, goodwill tax basis step-ups, recognition timing for tax law changes, and hybrid tax regime classification). No material impact on the consolidated financial statements.

- Note 3 — Restructuring and Impairment Charges (2019 Multi-Year Productivity Plan):
  - Plan aims to simplify, harmonize and automate processes; re-engineer go-to-market and information systems; and optimize manufacturing/supply chain. Extended through 2026.
  - Expected pre-tax charges increased to approximately $3.15 billion (about $2.4 billion cash), comprising ~55% severance/employee-related costs, ~10% non-cash asset impairments from plant actions, and ~35% other implementation costs.
  - Expected allocation of charges by division: FLNA 15%, QFNA 1%, PBNA 25%, LatAm 10%, Europe 25%, AMESA 5%, APAC 4%, Corporate 15%.
  - Annual restructuring/impairment charges: 2019 $370M, 2020 $289M, 2021 $247M; after-tax amounts $303M, $231M, $206M; EPS impact $(0.21), $(0.17), $(0.15), respectively.
  - Plan-to-date charges through 12/25/2021 total $1.044B: severance/employee $564M, asset impairments $157M, other costs $323M; divisional spend detailed (e.g., Europe $234M, FLNA $164M, PBNA $158M).
  - Restructuring liability rollforward shows ending accrual of $71M as of 12/25/2021; substantially all expected to be paid by end of 2022.

structure.title: Pension, Retiree Medical and Savings Plans
structure.heading: Note 7 — Pension, Retir ee Medical and Savings Plans
structure.start_phrase: In connection with our Juice Transaction subsequent to December 25, 2021, we transferred pension and retiree medical obligations of approximately $150 million and related assets to the newly formed joint venture.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Note 7 — Pension, Retiree Medical and Savings Plans, with detailed plan changes, funding, accounting, assumptions, asset allocations, and financials; begins Note 8 — Debt Obligations summarizing borrowings and maturities.

- Strategic actions and plan design changes:
  - Post–Dec 25, 2021 Juice Transaction: transferred ≈$150 million of pension and retiree medical obligations and related assets to a new JV.
  - 2021: Canada DB plans frozen for salaried participants effective Jan 1, 2024; hourly plan closed to new non-union hires from Jan 1, 2022. U.K. DB plan frozen for all participants effective Mar 31, 2022. Shift to employer DC contributions and match; pre-tax pension expense expected to decline post-effective dates, partially offset by higher DC contributions.
  - U.S.: Participant transfers from Plan A to Plan I effective Jan 1, 2022 (no benefit change; no material expense impact). Earlier actions include: freezing U.S. salaried DB accruals effective Dec 31, 2025 (reduced 2021 pre-tax pension expense by $70m); 2020 reorganization creating Plan H and moving some participants from Plan A to Plan I and Plan H (no material expense impact); enhanced Plan H pay credits effective Jan 1, 2021 (increased 2021 pre-tax pension expense by $45m).
  - Settlements: 2020 lump-sum activity triggered a $205m pre-tax settlement charge in Plan A; 2019 annuity purchase ($220m pre-tax settlement) and lump-sum offer ($53m pre-tax), totaling $273m pre-tax.

- Accounting policies:
  - Actuarial gains/losses recognized in AOCI; corridor method (>10%) amortized over average remaining service life or life expectancy (Plan A ≈9 yrs, Plan H ≈11 yrs, retiree medical ≈9 yrs, Plan I ≈27 yrs).
  - Prior service cost/credit amortized on a straight-line basis; salaried-freeze prior service amortized up to freeze effective date.

- Plan financials and funded status (2021 vs 2020):
  - U.S. pension: PBO $16.2b ($16.8b prior), plan assets $15.9b ($15.5b prior), funded status $(312)m (improved from $(1,288)m).
  - International pension: PBO $4.2b ($4.4b prior), plan assets $4.6b ($4.3b prior), funded status $449m (improved from $(127)m).
  - Retiree medical: obligation $954m ($1,006m prior), assets $299m ($315m prior), funded status $(655)m (vs $(691)m).
  - Net gains in the year primarily from higher discount rates, partially offset by demographic experience.

- Pension/retiree medical expense presentation:
  - Service cost reported in operating profit. Below operating profit: interest cost, expected return on assets, amortization of prior service and net losses/gains, settlement/curtailment, and special termination benefits. Tables provide 2019–2021 component details, including noted settlement charges.

- Assumptions:
  - 2021 weighted-average discount rates for PBO: U.S. pension 2.9%, International 2.4%, retiree medical 2.7%.
  - Expected long-term return on assets (2021): U.S. pension 6.4%, International 5.3%, retiree medical 5.4%.
  - Salary growth assumptions disclosed.

- Underfunded plans and funding approach:
  - Data on plans with ABO/PBO in excess of assets; decrease in U.S. plans under water driven by contributions to Plan H.
  - ≈$810m of PBO relates to plans not funded due to unfavorable tax treatment.

- Future cash flows:
  - Estimated benefit payments: pension $1.11b (2022) tapering annually, $5.385b (2027–2031); retiree medical $95m (2022) with Medicare subsidy note.
  - 2021 contributions: pension $738m (incl. $500m to U.S. qualified plans), retiree medical $47m. Expected 2022: U.S. pension discretionary $150m (split Jan/Q3), non-discretionary ≈$135m to U.S./int’l pension, ≈$55m retiree medical. Ongoing monitoring of COVID-19 impacts and de-risking opportunities.

- Plan assets and investment strategy:
  - Objectives: meet obligations, diversify across equities, high-quality debt, real estate; permitted use of derivatives (futures/forwards) to manage rate/FX risk.
  - U.S. expected return 6.3% (2022). Target allocation (2022/2021): fixed income 56%/51%, U.S. equity 22%/24%, international equity 18%/21%, real estate 4%/4%. Smoothing for non-fixed income returns over five years.
  - Fair value hierarchy and asset class breakdown provided for 2021/2020; retiree medical assets of $299m/$315m included.

- Retiree medical cost trend:
  - 2022 average increase assumption 6%, ultimate 4% by 2046; company cost cap limits impact.

- Savings plans:
  - U.S. 401(k) with company match based on service; additional employer contributions for salaried employees not in DB plan. Company contributions: $246m (2021), $225m (2020), $197m (2019).

- Debt obligations (beginning of Note 8):
  - 2021 short-term debt $4.3b (current maturities of LT debt $3.9b, commercial paper $0.4b, other $0.04b).
  - Long-term notes outstanding across 2022–2060 maturities totaling $39.9b gross; LT debt net of current maturities $36.0b (vs $40.4b in 2020). Rates shown are weighted-average effective; some fixed-rate debt swapped to floating. Small international borrowings via external lines of credit.

- Retiree medical cost trend assumptions:

  - 2021 long-term debt: $39.898B (less current maturities $3.872B = $36.026B); 2020: $43.728B (less $3.358B = $40.370B).

- 2021 financing activities:
  - Issued senior notes: €1.0B at 0.750% due 2033; $1.25B at 1.950% due 2031; $750M at 2.625% due 2041; $1.0B at 2.750% due 2051; proceeds for general corporate purposes including debt repurchases and commercial paper repayment.

  - New revolving credit facilities:

    - 364-Day Credit Agreement: up to $3.75B (USD/EUR), expandable to $4.5B, renewable or convertible to a term loan up to one year; replaces 2020 facility; no borrowings outstanding at 12/25/21.

- Other borrowings/redemptions:

  - 2020: Redeemed $1.1B 2.15% notes due 2020; terminated $0.8B swaps.
  - 2019: Redeemed $1.0B 4.50% notes due 2020.

- Financial instruments and hedging (Note 9):
  - Market risk exposures: commodity prices, foreign exchange (and currency restrictions), and interest rates.
  - Risk management via productivity initiatives, global purchasing (fixed-price contracts, purchase orders, pricing agreements), and hedging; no trading/speculation.
  - Use of derivatives and debt for hedging (including net investment hedges); some designated as cash flow or fair value hedges (hedge accounting applied), others marked to market through earnings; cash flow hedge results recognized in accumulated other comprehensive income.

structure.title: Financial Instruments
structure.heading: Note 9 — Financial Instruments
structure.start_phrase: We are exposed to market risks arising from adverse changes in:
structure.summary:
- Credit facilities and debt activity:
  - Entered a new Five-Year Credit Agreement in 2021 (replacing the 2019 $3.75 billion facility) and a new unsecured 364-Day Credit Agreement expiring May 27, 2022, allowing borrowings up to $3.75 billion in U.S. dollars/euros (up to $4.5 billion upon request), with options to renew or convert to a term loan; no borrowings outstanding under either as of December 25, 2021.
  - 2020 bridge loans (ZAR 21.7 billion, ~US$1.3 billion) used to fund the Pioneer Foods acquisition were fully repaid in April 2020.
  - Redeemed senior notes: $750 million (1.70% due 2021) in 2021; $1.1 billion (2.15% due 2020) in 2020; $1.0 billion (4.50% due 2020) in 2019; associated interest rate swaps were terminated.

- Derivatives and hedging framework (Note 9):
  - Risks managed: commodity prices, foreign exchange, and interest rates via productivity initiatives, global purchasing, and derivatives; no trading/speculation.
  - Hedge accounting applied for qualifying cash flow and fair value hedges; gains/losses recognized in AOCI and reclassified when hedged items affect earnings; derivative cash flows classified in operating activities consistent with hedged items.
  - Counterparty credit risk considered low; agreements may require collateral posting upon rating downgrades (A2/A thresholds); as of year-end 2021, $247 million net liability position with credit-contingent features, no collateral posted.

- Commodity price risk:
  - Managed with fixed-price contracts and derivatives (swaps/futures) with terms up to three years.
  - Non-qualifying hedges are marked to market in corporate unallocated expenses and later reflected in division results.
  - Notional value of commodity derivatives: $1.6 billion (2021) vs. $1.1 billion (2020).

- Foreign exchange risk:
  - Managed through local sourcing, contracts in local currencies, and forward contracts (terms up to two years); use of net investment hedges (debt).
  - FX derivative notional: $2.8 billion (2021) vs. $1.9 billion (2020).
  - Debt designated as net investment hedges: $2.1 billion (2021) vs. $2.7 billion (2020).
  - Non-qualifying hedge gains/losses offset underlying items with no material net earnings impact.

- Interest rate risk:
  - Use of interest rate swaps, cross-currency swaps, Treasury locks, and swap locks to manage interest expense and FX risk; some fixed-rate debt swapped to floating; swaps match debt terms.
  - Interest rate derivative notional: $2.1 billion (2021) vs. $3.0 billion (2020).
  - Variable-rate debt exposure: ~2% (2021) vs. ~3% (2020), after derivatives.

- Held-to-maturity debt securities:
  - Consist of U.S. Treasury securities and commercial paper; maturities less than one year; carried at amortized cost with immaterial unrealized amounts.
  - 2021: $130 million commercial paper; no Treasuries.
  - 2020: $2.1 billion U.S. Treasuries and $260 million commercial paper.

- Fair value measurements:
  - Disclosures by hierarchy: Level 1 index fund assets; Level 2 prepaid forwards, deferred compensation liabilities, and derivatives; Level 3 contingent consideration.
  - Rockstar acquisition contingent consideration (tax-related, up to ~$1.1 billion): option exercised in Q4 2021 to accelerate all remaining payments; $773 million paid; recognized pre-tax gain of $86 million; small fair value decrease recorded in goodwill.
  - Derivatives presented gross; fair value of total debt: $43 billion (2021) vs. $50 billion (2020).

- Hedge results and outlook:
  - Tables summarize 2021 vs. 2020 gains/losses on fair value/non-designated hedges and cash flow/net investment hedges across FX, interest, and commodities.
  - Expect to reclassify net gains of $176 million from AOCI to net income in the next 12 months.

- Earnings per share (Note 10):
  - Basic EPS: $5.51 (2021), $5.14 (2020), $5.23 (2019).
  - Diluted EPS: $5.49 (2021), $5.12 (2020), $5.20 (2019).
  - Dilutive securities include stock options and share units; antidilutive securities immaterial.

structure.title: Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss Attributable to PepsiCo
structure.heading: Note 1 1 — Accumulated Other Compr ehensive Loss Attributable to PepsiCo
structure.start_phrase: The changes in the balances of each component of accumulated other comprehensive loss attributable to PepsiCo are as follows:
structure.summary:
- Accumulated Other Comprehensive Loss (AOCI) rollforward: Details the components of AOCI attributable to PepsiCo—currency translation adjustments, cash flow hedges, pension and retiree medical, and other—from year-end 2018 through year-end 2021. For each year, shows other comprehensive income/(loss) before reclassifications, amounts reclassified to earnings, related tax effects, and ending balances.
- Key drivers and disclosures:
  - 2021 “Other” primarily reflects fair value increases in available-for-sale securities.
  - Pension and retiree medical amounts are presented net of specified tax amounts for each year.
  - Currency translation effects are explained by notable currency movements by year (e.g., appreciation/depreciation of the Russian ruble, Canadian dollar, Mexican peso, Pound sterling, Turkish lira, and Swiss franc).
- Reclassifications from AOCI to the income statement (2019–2021): Summarizes amounts reclassified and the impacted income statement lines.
  - Currency translation reclassifications tied to divestitures (to SG&A).
  - Cash flow hedges: foreign exchange contracts (to Net revenue and Cost of sales), interest rate derivatives (to SG&A), and commodity contracts (to Cost of sales and SG&A), with net gains/losses presented before and after tax.
  - Pension and retiree medical: amortization of prior service credits and net losses, and settlement/curtailment losses (to other pension and retiree medical benefits income/expense), with totals before and after tax and the total net losses reclassified for each year.
- Leases (Lessee) accounting policy:
  - Determines lease existence at inception; primarily operating leases for facilities and equipment (including fleet) with remaining terms up to 20 years, options to extend (up to five years) or terminate (within one year), which are considered in measuring right-of-use assets and lease liabilities.
  - Uses incremental borrowing rate when no implicit rate is available.
  - For real estate, accounts for lease and non-lease components together (e.g., common-area maintenance).
  - Lease agreements have no material residual value guarantees or restrictive covenants.

- Summarizes reclassifications from accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) to the income statement for 2019–2021:

  - Cash flow hedges by instrument and affected line items: foreign exchange contracts (net revenue and cost of sales), interest rate derivatives (SG&A), and commodity contracts (cost of sales and SG&A).
  - Pre-tax and after-tax net (gains)/losses from these hedges (e.g., net after-tax gains of $37 million in 2021 and $87 million in 2020, versus a $12 million loss in 2019).
  - Pension and retiree medical items reclassified: amortization of prior service credit and net losses, and settlement/curtailment losses, with related tax effects; net losses after tax of $234 million (2021), $364 million (2020), and $366 million (2019).
  - Total net losses reclassified, net of tax: $215 million (2021), $277 million (2020), $378 million (2019).

- Note 12 — Leases (Lessee and Lessor):
  - Lessee policies and portfolio: operating leases for facilities and equipment with remaining terms up to 20 years; use of incremental borrowing rate; consideration of extension/termination options; combining lease and non-lease components for real estate.
  - Lease costs (2019–2021): operating, variable, and short-term lease costs; includes right-of-use (ROU) asset amortization; variable costs mainly inflation/CAM/property taxes; short-term costs off-balance sheet.
  - Sale-leaseback gains recognized (terms under five years) in 2019–2021.
  - Cash flow and non-cash data: cash paid for lease liabilities and ROU assets obtained in exchange for lease obligations.
  - Balance sheet (2021 vs. 2020): ROU assets of $2.02 billion (vs. $1.67 billion); current lease liabilities $446 million (vs. $460 million); non-current $1.598 billion (vs. $1.233 billion).

structure.start_phrase: We have audited the accompanying Consolidated Balance Sheet of PepsiCo, Inc. and Subsidiaries (the Company) as of December 25, 2021 and December 26, 2020, the related Consolidated Statements of Income,
structure.summary:
- Independent auditor’s report from KPMG to PepsiCo’s shareholders and board covering:
  - Unqualified opinions on the consolidated financial statements for fiscal years in the three-year period ended Dec 25, 2021, and on internal control over financial reporting (ICFR) as of Dec 25, 2021.
  - ICFR assessment based on COSO 2013; financial statements prepared in conformity with U.S. GAAP.

- Basis for opinions:
  - Management’s responsibility for the financial statements and ICFR; auditor’s responsibility to express opinions.
  - Auditor independence under SEC and PCAOB rules.
  - Audits conducted under PCAOB standards, providing reasonable assurance via risk assessment, testing, evaluation of accounting principles, significant estimates, overall presentation, and ICFR design/operating effectiveness.

- Definition and limitations of ICFR:
  - Objectives (reliable reporting, GAAP-compliant statements, authorized transactions, safeguarding of assets).
  - Inherent limitations and the risk that control effectiveness may change over time.

- Critical Audit Matters (CAMs) identified:
  1) Sales incentive accruals:
     - Complexity due to timing of incentives vs. deliveries and reliance on participation/performance forecasts and historical trends.
     - Procedures included control testing, trend analyses, recalculations, back-testing prior accruals to settlements, and testing post-period settlements.
  2) Carrying value of certain indefinite-lived intangibles:
     - PBNA reacquired/acquired franchise rights and certain Europe juice/dairy brands in Russia; significant judgments in cash flow forecasts, growth rates, discount rates, and competitive/macro factors.
     - Procedures included control testing, sensitivity analyses, forecast back-testing, comparisons to external industry/economic data, and use of valuation specialists.
  3) Unrecognized tax benefits:
     - Complexity and subjectivity in applying tax law and interpreting tax authority practices; impacts timing and amounts of reserves.
     - Procedures included control testing, involvement of tax specialists, assessment of structure/transfer pricing, review of laws, rulings, examinations, settlements, and counsel opinions.

- Auditor tenure and sign-off: KPMG LLP, auditor since 1990; New York, February 9, 2022.

- Glossary:
  - Definitions of key operating and financial terms used by PepsiCo, including Acquisitions and divestitures, Bottler Case Sales (BCS), Bottler funding, Concentrate Shipments and Equivalents (CSE), Constant currency, Consumers, CSD, Customers, Direct-Store-Delivery (DSD), Effective net pricing, Free cash flow, Independent bottlers, Mark-to-market net impact, Organic, Total marketplace spending, and Transaction gains and losses.

nodes.title: Proxy Access.
